short: An interview that asks every candidate the same job-related questions in the same order and scores each answer on the same anchored scale; the most valid single predictor in the 2022 re-estimation.
definition: A structured interview measures job-related competencies by asking every candidate the same predetermined questions in the same order and scoring every answer on the same rating scale, with behavioral (past experience) and situational (hypothetical) question types [41](#cite:41). In the 2022 re-estimation of selection validity it is the most valid single predictor, at an operational validity of .42, and it carries a Black–White standardized difference of .23, smaller than tests of job knowledge (.54) or cognitive ability (.79) [1](#cite:1). The structure effect in its original form was .44 for structured against .33 for unstructured interviews in the 1994 interview meta-analysis [5](#cite:5). Its validity varies between studies, so the mean is not a guarantee [3](#cite:3); once the range restriction of using the interview as a first screen is corrected, two behavioral interview forms showed d of .36 and .56 [18](#cite:18); and formal interviewer training was the modifiable antecedent of using the components that carry its validity among 131 professional interviewers [19](#cite:19).

short: A conversational interview without fixed questions or a scoring scale; it predicts job performance at .19 in the 2022 re-estimation and dilutes stronger evidence when added to it.
definition: An unstructured interview has no fixed question set and no written rating scale, the defining absence that the structured-interview literature identifies [41](#cite:41) [6](#cite:6). The 2022 re-estimation puts its operational validity at .19 against .42 for structured interviews, down from the .38 carried in the 1998 baseline [1](#cite:1) [4](#cite:4). Adding unstructured interview ratings to valid test scores lowered decision accuracy while raising confidence among hiring decision-makers [9](#cite:9), and in laboratory studies interviewers formed confident impressions from random answers and could not tell random interviews from real ones, which the authors attribute to sensemaking and dilution [8](#cite:8). Hiring managers who overrode a valid test on their own read of the candidate made worse hires on average across fifteen service-sector firms [10](#cite:10).

short: The validity a meta-analysis reports for a selection method against job performance after its corrections; the 2022 re-estimation revised the main figures downward by .10 to .20.
definition: Operational validity is the figure the pack quotes for how well a selection method predicts job performance, as a meta-analysis reports it after the corrections it applies for criterion unreliability and range restriction [3](#cite:3) [1](#cite:1). The 2022 re-estimation showed that prior meta-analyses had applied range-restriction corrections derived from predictive studies to the concurrent studies that dominate the databases, which overcorrected; with no correction for concurrent studies the revised estimates fall by .10 to .20 while the rank order of the strong predictors largely holds [1](#cite:1). The revised values put structured interviews at .42, job knowledge tests at .40, empirically keyed biodata at .38, work samples at .33, cognitive ability at .31, unstructured interviews at .19 and years of experience at .07 [1](#cite:1). The published rebuttal argues that range restriction in concurrent studies is larger than the authors assume [2](#cite:2).

short: The narrowing of score variance when only screened or incumbent people are studied; how far to correct for it is the dispute behind the 2022 revision of selection validity.
definition: Range restriction is the narrowing of predictor variance in a validation sample whose members already passed a cutoff or are incumbents, and meta-analyses correct for it; the 2022 re-estimation found that earlier corrections had applied predictive-study assumptions to concurrent studies of incumbents, which overcorrected, and recommended no range-restriction correction for concurrent studies [1](#cite:1) [24](#cite:24). The authors held that restriction in concurrent studies is small unless the selection variable correlates about .90 with the predictor and selection ratios are .30 or lower; the published rebuttal argues both conditions are plausible and that the no-correction recommendation lacks support [2](#cite:2). The same correction cuts the other way for group differences: once the restriction from using an interview as an initial screen is corrected, two behavioral interview forms showed Black–White d of .36 and .56 [18](#cite:18), and the apparent differential validity of cognitive tests by subgroup is largely an artifact of differential range restriction [24](#cite:24).

short: Validity evidence showing that scores on a selection procedure relate to measures of job performance; one of the three strategies the Uniform Guidelines accept.
definition: Criterion-related validity is the first of the three validation strategies the Uniform Guidelines accept, alongside content and construct validity; each must be tied to important elements of job performance and aligned with generally accepted professional standards [32](#cite:32). The evidence may come from a predictive study or from a concurrent study of incumbents, and the 2022 re-estimation turned on the difference, since the range-restriction corrections built for predictive studies had been applied to the concurrent studies that dominate the meta-analytic databases [1](#cite:1). The EEOC's fact sheet adds that an employer must validate for the specific job and purpose and remains responsible for validation even when a vendor supplied the test [33](#cite:33), and the SIOP Principles are the professional standard for what validated means [29](#cite:29).

short: A test of general mental ability; moved from the focal predictor (.51) to a mid-table one (.31) in the 2022 re-estimation, and the predictor with the largest Black–White difference (d .79).
definition: A cognitive ability test measures general mental ability, which the 1998 synthesis made the focal predictor of job performance at a validity of .51, with its best pairings an integrity test (R = .65), a work sample (.63) or a structured interview (.63) [4](#cite:4). The 2022 re-estimation puts cognitive ability at .31, well down the list behind structured interviews, job knowledge tests, biodata and work samples, and pairs it with a Black–White d of .79, the largest of any common predictor [1](#cite:1). The published rebuttal disputes the no-correction reasoning behind the fall [2](#cite:2), and the pack carries the dispute as the cognitive-ability-validity controversy, in which both sides agree that structure beats judgment and that a cognitive test adds the largest group difference [1](#cite:1) [4](#cite:4). Applicants rate cognitive tests in the middle of the selection procedures (3.14 on a five-point scale) [14](#cite:14), and the reviewed remedies for the group difference include alternative cognitive measures and simulations with low cognitive load [25](#cite:25).

short: A test in which candidates perform a sample of the actual work, scored against a standard; validity .33 in the 2022 re-estimation with a Black–White d of .67.
definition: A work sample test has candidates do a sample of the actual work and scores it against a standard [17](#cite:17). The 2022 re-estimation puts its operational validity at .33 (k = 54, N = 10,469), down from the .54 of the 1998 baseline, with a Black–White d of .67, so it is better used as a pass/fail prerequisite than for ranking, which the Uniform Guidelines treat as needing more validity evidence [1](#cite:1) [4](#cite:4) [32](#cite:32). Applicants rate work samples second only to interviews for favorability (3.63 on a five-point scale) [14](#cite:14). The evidence summary the pack carries says to derive the sample from a job analysis, standardize administration and scoring, test the prerequisites that will not be trained, and get expert help because development is technically demanding [17](#cite:17); the complaint developers make about live-coding interviews is that the exercise is a puzzle the role never poses [22](#cite:22).

short: A test of the knowledge a job requires; second to the structured interview in the 2022 re-estimation at .40, with a Black–White d of .54.
definition: A job knowledge test measures the knowledge the job requires, scored against a standard; its operational validity is .40 in the 2022 re-estimation (k = 59, N = 3,965), down from .48 in the 1998 baseline, and its Black–White d is .54 [1](#cite:1) [4](#cite:4). Because of that difference the lever record keeps it, with the work sample, to pass/fail use, since the Uniform Guidelines ask for more validity evidence where ranking has more adverse impact [32](#cite:32). The convenient proxy it stands against, years of experience, carries an operational validity of .07 [1](#cite:1).

short: Scored biographical information about a candidate; empirically keyed biodata predicts at .38 in the 2022 re-estimation and is among the procedures applicants like least.
definition: Biodata is scored biographical information, and the 2022 re-estimation puts empirically keyed biodata at an operational validity of .38 (k = 49, N = 20,564), up from the 1998 baseline of .35 against the general downward revision, with a Black–White d of .33 [1](#cite:1) [4](#cite:4). Applicants rate it among the least favored procedures, at 2.81 on a five-point scale, below cognitive tests and above personal contacts and honesty tests [14](#cite:14). The pack carries no lever built on it.

short: A selection test the 2022 re-estimation lists as SJT (knowledge) at an operational validity of .26, with a Black–White d of .39; no lever in the pack rests on it.
definition: The situational judgment test appears in the pack only in the 2022 re-estimation, which lists the knowledge-type SJT at an operational validity of .26 and a Black–White d of .39, below structured interviews, job knowledge tests, biodata, work samples, cognitive ability, integrity tests and assessment centers in the revised ordering and above interests and unstructured interviews [1](#cite:1). No lever, constraint or applicant-reaction figure in the pack rests on it, so the pack says nothing about how one is built or how applicants receive it.

short: A test of honesty or integrity; .31 validity with one of the smallest Black–White differences (d .10) in the 2022 re-estimation, and one of the procedures applicants like least.
definition: An integrity test, which the applicant-reactions literature calls an honesty test, carries an operational validity of .31 in the 2022 re-estimation with a Black–White d of .10, among the smallest in the table [1](#cite:1). The 1998 baseline put it at .41 and named cognitive ability plus an integrity test the best two-predictor combination (R = .65) [4](#cite:4). Applicants rate honesty tests near the bottom of the selection procedures, 2.47 on a five-point scale, above only graphology [14](#cite:14), and the EEOC counts personality and integrity tests among the selection procedures its fact sheet covers [33](#cite:33).

short: A selection method listed in the 2022 re-estimation at .29 operational validity with a Black–White d of .52, down from .37 in the 1998 baseline.
definition: The assessment center is listed in the 2022 re-estimation at an operational validity of .29 with a Black–White d of .52, which places it below cognitive ability and integrity tests on validity and among the predictors with large group differences [1](#cite:1). The 1998 baseline carried it at .37 [4](#cite:4). The pack carries no lever built on it and no applicant-reaction figure for it.

short: A test of traits such as conscientiousness; conscientiousness predicts at .19 in the 2022 re-estimation with a negligible group difference, and applicants rate personality tests low.
definition: Personality tests are among the selection procedures the EEOC's fact sheet covers [33](#cite:33), and the 2022 re-estimation carries conscientiousness, the trait the pack has figures for, at an operational validity of .19 with a Black–White d of −.07, the only negative difference in the table [1](#cite:1). The 1998 baseline had put conscientiousness at .31 [4](#cite:4). Applicants rate personality tests at 2.88 on a five-point scale, below cognitive tests and interviews [14](#cite:14), and HR professionals place far less faith in intelligence and personality tests than the research supports [20](#cite:20). Under the ADA a psychological test is a medical examination, barred before a conditional offer, if it can identify a mental disorder [34](#cite:34).

short: How applicants perceive a selection procedure; perceptions predict attraction, offer acceptance and withdrawal, and interviews and work samples are the best liked.
definition: Applicant reactions are the perceptions applicants form of a selection process, and across 86 independent samples (N = 48,750) they correlate with organizational attractiveness, intention to accept an offer and willingness to recommend the employer, at average r from .08 to .52, while being almost unrelated to gender, age and ethnicity [14](#cite:14). Interviews (3.84 on a five-point scale) and work samples (3.63) are rated most favorably; cognitive tests sit in the middle (3.14); personality tests (2.88), biodata (2.81), honesty tests (2.47) and graphology (1.76) are least liked, and face validity and perceived predictive validity drive the justice judgments [14](#cite:14). Withdrawal from a multi-stage process tracked perceptions of the organization and the hiring process among 3,550 police applicants [16](#cite:16).

short: Telling candidates the hard parts of the job and the firm before they decide; across 40 studies previews lowered inflated expectations and turnover, mainly by signaling honesty.
definition: A realistic job preview tells candidates the hard parts of the job and the firm before they decide, which for a customer-governed firm means the hours, the site, the customer, the clearance wait and the pay range (the lever `l-realistic-job-preview`). Across 40 studies previews lowered initial expectations, attrition during recruiting and voluntary and total turnover, with timing and medium as moderators [12](#cite:12). Across 52 studies and about 17,000 participants the effect ran mainly through perceived organizational honesty, with oral or written previews delivered after hiring the most effective [13](#cite:13). The EEOC counts realistic job previews among the work samples and simulations it treats as selection procedures [33](#cite:33). The numeric effect sizes were not read, so the pack quotes the direction and not the magnitude [12](#cite:12).

short: Combining predictor scores by formula and treating the total as the anchor for the decision; it predicts job performance at r .44 against .28 for judgment.
definition: Mechanical combination scores each predictor, weights and adds the scores, and treats the total as the anchor for the decision. Across nine job-performance comparisons (N = 1,392 mechanical and 1,156 clinical), the same predictor information combined by formula predicted job performance at r .44 (cross-validated .40) against .28 when combined holistically [7](#cite:7). The authors conclude that experts collect information well and combine it poorly, and recommend screening mechanically, using the mechanical score as the anchor for any adjustment, documenting deviations and averaging across raters [7](#cite:7). Managers who overrode a job test's recommendation across fifteen service-sector firms made worse hires on average [10](#cite:10). A formula built on a weak proxy such as years of experience (.07) is a precise way of being wrong [1](#cite:1).

short: Combining selection evidence holistically, by judgment or feel instead of by formula; it costs more than a third of the achievable validity (r .28 against .44).
definition: Clinical judgment is the holistic combination of selection evidence by a decision-maker's judgment, the method the meta-analysis of mechanical versus clinical data combination compares against formula [7](#cite:7). For job performance the clinical combination of the same predictors reached r .28 against .44 mechanically, a consistent and substantial loss of validity, probably underestimated because no corrections were possible [7](#cite:7). The mechanisms that keep it credible are sensemaking, by which an interviewer builds a coherent story from almost anything, and dilution, by which weak information crowds out strong [8](#cite:8); hiring decision-makers who saw unstructured interview ratings beside test scores predicted worse and were more overconfident [9](#cite:9). In the pack it is the constraint `c-unstructured-judgement`.

short: The standardized gap (d) between group means on a predictor; cognitive ability tests show the largest Black–White d (.79) and structured interviews one of the smallest (.23).
definition: A subgroup difference is the standardized difference (d) between the mean scores of two groups on a predictor, and the 2022 re-estimation pairs each validity with a Black–White d so that the validity–diversity trade-off is visible: cognitive ability .79, work samples .67, job knowledge .54, assessment centers .52, years of experience .49, SJT .39, biodata .33, unstructured interviews .32, structured interviews .23, integrity .10 and conscientiousness −.07 [1](#cite:1). The d values mix applicant, incumbent and national samples and are offered to locate predictors as having large, modest or minimal group differences [1](#cite:1). Corrected for the range restriction of using the interview as a first screen, two behavioral interview forms showed d of .36 and .56 [18](#cite:18). The reviewed remedies are simulations with low cognitive load and high fidelity, alternative cognitive measures and Pareto-optimal predictor weighting [25](#cite:25), and an NLP screen reduced minority–nonminority differences in board scores across four samples (N = 1,828) [23](#cite:23).

short: A substantially lower rate of selection for a race, sex or ethnic group; under the Uniform Guidelines a rate below four-fifths of the highest group's is generally regarded as evidence of it.
definition: Adverse impact is a substantially lower selection rate for a race, sex or ethnic group, and the Uniform Guidelines treat a selection rate below four-fifths of the highest group's as generally regarded as evidence of it, qualified by statistical and practical significance and by small numbers [31](#cite:31) [35](#cite:35). Employers keep records of selection rates by sex and by race or ethnic group, and where the overall process shows no adverse impact the agencies generally do not expect component evaluation [31](#cite:31). A procedure with adverse impact needs criterion-related, content or construct validity evidence tied to important elements of job performance, with more evidence for ranking than for pass/fail use [32](#cite:32). An algorithmic tool used to make or inform a selection decision is a selection procedure under the same rules, and the employer answers for a vendor's tool [35](#cite:35).

short: The Uniform Guidelines' rule of thumb: a group's selection rate below four-fifths (eighty percent) of the highest group's is generally regarded as evidence of adverse impact.
definition: The four-fifths rule compares each group's selection rate to the highest group's; a rate 'less than four-fifths (4/5) (or eighty percent)' of the highest is generally regarded by the enforcement agencies as evidence of adverse impact, while smaller differences may still count where they are statistically and practically significant and larger ones may not where numbers are small [31](#cite:31). The EEOC's withdrawn 2023 technical assistance called it a rule of thumb and not a legal definition, so that compliance with it does not prove lawfulness, and courts have declined to treat it as conclusive [35](#cite:35). With small applicant pools the rule is unreliable and the Guidelines say agencies may look at longer periods or at similar uses elsewhere [31](#cite:31).

variants: Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures
short: The 1978 framework (29 CFR 1607) the EEOC, DOL, DOJ and the Civil Service Commission adopted for judging selection procedures under Title VII: records by group, the four-fifths test, validation.
definition: The Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, 29 CFR Part 1607, are the framework adopted on August 25, 1978 by the EEOC, the Civil Service Commission, the Department of Labor and the Department of Justice for judging selection procedures under Title VII, eighteen sections resting on sections 709 and 713 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 [30](#cite:30). Section 1607.4 expects records of selection rates by sex and by race or ethnic group and sets the four-fifths rule of thumb and the bottom-line rule [31](#cite:31); section 1607.5 accepts criterion-related, content or construct validity tied to important elements of job performance, cutoffs set to normal expectations of acceptable proficiency, and more evidence for ranking than for pass/fail use [32](#cite:32). An algorithmic tool used to make or inform a selection decision is a selection procedure under the Guidelines [35](#cite:35). They are the governing text of the select stage, the gate `ugesp`.

short: A study showing that a selection procedure relates to job performance; predictive studies follow applicants, concurrent studies test incumbents, and the two need different corrections.
definition: A validation study produces the evidence the Uniform Guidelines require for a procedure with adverse impact: criterion-related, content or construct validity tied to important elements of job performance and consistent with generally accepted professional standards [32](#cite:32). The standard the agencies and courts refer to is the SIOP Principles, adopted as APA policy in 2018 [29](#cite:29). The 2022 re-estimation distinguishes predictive studies from the concurrent studies of incumbents that dominate the meta-analytic databases and recommends no range-restriction correction for the concurrent ones [1](#cite:1). The employer remains responsible for validation even when a vendor supplied the tool and should obtain its documentation [33](#cite:33); California's regulations treat anti-bias testing before and after adoption of an automated-decision system as a defense factor [40](#cite:40).

short: The study of a job from which selection criteria, interview competencies and work samples are derived; the Uniform Guidelines tie validity to important elements of job performance.
definition: A job analysis is the study of the job from which the pack's selection levers are built: the Uniform Guidelines tie validity evidence to important elements of job performance [32](#cite:32), the structured-interview method defines competencies from the job before writing its questions [41](#cite:41), and a work sample is derived from a job analysis and then standardized in administration and scoring [17](#cite:17). A screen whose criteria were never tied to a job analysis defaults to the convenient proxies, and years of experience carries an operational validity of .07 [1](#cite:1). A requirement in a posting that cannot be traced to the contract's labor category, to the customer in writing or to a job analysis is the plan-stage constraint `c-preferences-written-as-requirements` [32](#cite:32) [99](#cite:99).

short: A requirement the job actually needs, as distinct from a preference inherited from the customer or an incumbent; the guide asks that each be labeled contractual, customer-required or preferred.
definition: An essential requirement is one the opening actually needs, which in a customer-governed requisition has three possible sources: the contract's labor category, whose qualification line is enforceable because hours by people who do not meet it are not paid [99](#cite:99); a customer requirement stated in writing, which the personal-services rule lets the customer apply to the result but not to the supervision of the hire [197](#cite:197); and the firm's own preference. The lever `l-requisition-scorecard-with-customer` labels each requirement as contractual, customer-required in writing or preferred and names who can waive it [99](#cite:99) [197](#cite:197). A requirement with adverse impact must be job-related and consistent with business necessity [30](#cite:30) [32](#cite:32); years of experience predicts performance at .07 [1](#cite:1); and roles that dropped degree lines rose almost fourfold from 2014 to 2023 while non-degree hiring in them rose only 3.5 percentage points, because the screens did not change [68](#cite:68).

short: The live-coding or whiteboard interview used for software roles; in a randomized trial being watched halved performance on the same problem and raised measured stress.
definition: The technical interview, in the form the pack has evidence on, is live coding on a whiteboard while being watched. In a randomized trial of 48 computer-science students it halved performance on the same problem relative to solving it privately and raised measured stress and cognitive load, which the authors read as the format confounding problem-solving with performance anxiety [21](#cite:21). Developers on a large practitioner forum describe the format as unrelated to real work, biased toward the young and recently drilled, time-consuming, anxiety-provoking and governed by unwritten norms [22](#cite:22). The alternatives the studies propose are a private focus session with retrospective think-aloud and collaborative problem-solving [21](#cite:21) [22](#cite:22); the validity still has to come from the exercise being a sample of the job [1](#cite:1) [17](#cite:17). In the pack it is the constraint `c-technical-interview-measures-anxiety`.

short: Days from requisition opening to accepted offer; the 2025 SHRM median is about 45 days for executive and nonexecutive roles alike.
definition: Time to fill is the number of days from the opening of a requisition to an accepted offer, the select stage's first metric. The 2025 SHRM benchmark puts the median at about 45 days for executive and nonexecutive roles, after executive roles took 16 to 17 days longer in 2017 and 2022 [43](#cite:43); the 2025 benchmarking brief reports about a month and a half overall and 45 days for executive roles, down from 60 [196](#cite:196). The one public figure for cleared technical roles is a vendor survey of 2021 giving 41 to 60 days for a cleared IT role [88](#cite:88). The figure is the vacancy window against which the DCSA industry clearance clock of 197 to 243 days is measured [126](#cite:126) [125](#cite:125) [43](#cite:43). ISO technical specifications define cost per hire, impact of hire and quality of hire [46](#cite:46).

short: A recruiting metric the pack carries no definition or benchmark for; the measure the pack's records carry is time to fill, a 2025 median of about 45 days.
definition: Time to hire is a recruiting metric that none of the pack's records or references defines or benchmarks; the measure the pack carries is time to fill, the days from requisition opening to accepted offer, with a 2025 median of about 45 days in the SHRM benchmark [43](#cite:43). The ISO technical specifications the pack cites define cost per hire, impact of hire and quality of hire, and the successor to the withdrawn ISO 30414 standard is a todo [46](#cite:46). Where the pack measures the candidate's own clock it does so from acceptance onward, as the offer-to-start interval, in which each additional week raised the odds of a no-show by 22 percent in the one field study [144](#cite:144).

short: Candidates who stop responding during the process or after accepting; 41 percent of organizations reported it rising in 2025.
definition: Candidate ghosting is the candidate who stops responding, during the process or after accepting an offer. In the 2025 SHRM benchmark 41 percent of organizations cited rising candidate ghosting, the closest published figure to a withdrawal rate, alongside a median time to fill of about 45 days [43](#cite:43). The pack's only field evidence on withdrawal before a decision found that those who withdrew from a multiple-hurdle process differed from those who stayed on their perceptions of the organization and the process, career commitment, current employment, relocation and the views of family and friends, with early and late withdrawers differing [16](#cite:16), and earlier post-interview offers were more often accepted [15](#cite:15). The accepted hire who never starts is the pack's new-hire no-show, which the one field study calls new hire ghosting: 4.1 percent of 157,154 accepted offers at one employer [144](#cite:144).

short: An accepted hire who never starts; 4.1 percent of 157,154 accepted offers at one employer, with each week between acceptance and start raising the odds by about a fifth.
definition: A new-hire no-show is an accepted offer that never becomes a first day. Among 157,154 accepted entry-level offers at one telecommunications employer between May 2019 and June 2025, 4.1 percent of hires never showed (a peak of 6.1 percent in April 2020), and each additional week between acceptance and the start date raised the odds by about a fifth (OR 1.22) [144](#cite:144). In the companion survey a referral (OR 0.42), good company communication (OR 0.56) and financial security (OR 0.86) lowered the odds while an external offer (OR 1.18) raised them, and the reasons given were another job (39 percent), pay (29 percent) and a negative perception of the company (24 percent) [144](#cite:144). The population is entry-level and customer-facing, so the rates do not transfer to cleared technical hiring; the mechanism is what the pack carries, as the constraint `c-long-interval-loses-accepted-hires` [144](#cite:144). A cleared opening stretches the interval to the clearance clock, 197 to 243 days on the current figures [126](#cite:126) [125](#cite:125).

short: Offers accepted over offers extended; in the one field study earlier post-interview offers were more often accepted, with no later performance or turnover penalty.
definition: The offer acceptance rate is offers accepted over offers extended, the offer stage's first metric. In the one field study of offer timing, archival data on 3,012 candidates at one large company (906 students and 2,106 experienced), earlier post-interview offers were more likely to be accepted in both pools, and hires made on fast offers performed and stayed no differently from those hired on slow ones [15](#cite:15). Favorable perceptions of the selection process predict intention to accept an offer [14](#cite:14), and an accepted offer is not a start, since 58 percent of senior managers in one staffing-firm survey extend counteroffers [113](#cite:113) and 4.1 percent of accepted offers at one employer never started [144](#cite:144). The acceptance effect sizes were not read, so the pack quotes the direction and not the magnitude [15](#cite:15).

short: A published pooling of many studies' effect sizes; the guide's highest evidence grade, quoted with its k and N as reported.
definition: A meta-analysis is a published synthesis that pools the effect sizes of many studies, and in the pack's evidence grades it is the strongest grade, defined in scope.yaml as a published meta-analysis or systematic review whose effect size is quoted with its k and N as reported. The pack's selection evidence rests on them: the 2022 re-estimation of selection validity pools prior databases such as the structured-interview sets of k = 36 with N = 3,069 and k = 69 with N = 4,795 [1](#cite:1); the mechanical-versus-clinical comparison draws on nine job-performance studies [7](#cite:7); the applicant-reactions synthesis covers 86 samples (N = 48,750) [14](#cite:14); the turnover synthesis covers 316 studies [178](#cite:178). A meta-analytic estimate is a mean, and the 2022 authors argue for attending to its variability as well [3](#cite:3).

short: The size of a relationship or difference as a study reports it (a correlation, a d, an odds ratio, a percentage); the guide quotes each exactly, with its population and statistic.
definition: An effect size is the magnitude a study reports for a relationship or a difference, and the pack's standing rule is that effect sizes are quoted exactly as reported, with population and statistic. The statistics the pack carries are validity coefficients and corrected correlations, such as .42 for structured interviews [1](#cite:1); observed correlations such as r .44 for mechanical combination [7](#cite:7); standardized mean differences such as the Black–White d of .79 for cognitive ability [1](#cite:1); odds ratios such as 1.22 per week of offer-to-start interval [144](#cite:144); and percentages such as the more than 10 percent rise in median tenure after a retailer adopted testing [11](#cite:11). Where a reference was read only in abstract the effect size is a todo and the pack quotes the direction without a magnitude [12](#cite:12) [15](#cite:15).

short: A measure of how closely two quantities move together, written r when observed and ρ when corrected; the guide's validity figures and turnover predictors are correlations.
definition: A correlation coefficient measures how closely two quantities move together, and most of the pack's effect sizes are correlations: the selection validities are correlations between a predictor and job performance, reported as operational validities after correction [1](#cite:1); the mechanical-versus-clinical comparison reports r .44 against .28 [7](#cite:7); the applicant-reactions synthesis reports average r from .08 to .52 between perceptions and outcomes [14](#cite:14). The turnover predictors are corrected correlations written ρ, with withdrawal cognitions at .56, job search at .40 and pay at −.17 [178](#cite:178), and the unit-level synthesis reports turnover rates at about −.22 with customer satisfaction and production efficiency and −.15 with profit margin [181](#cite:181). A negative sign means the two move in opposite directions, as pay and quitting do [178](#cite:178).

short: The ratio of the odds of an outcome between two conditions; 1.22 per extra week of offer-to-start interval means each week raised the odds of a no-show by about a fifth.
definition: An odds ratio (OR) compares the odds of an outcome under one condition with the odds under another; an OR above 1 raises the odds and one below 1 lowers them. The pack's no-show evidence is reported this way: each additional week between acceptance and start carried an OR of 1.22 for ghosting, a referral 0.42, company communication quality 0.56, financial security 0.86, an external offer 1.18 and impulsivity 2.05 [144](#cite:144). The onboarding evidence from one financial-services employer is also in odds ratios: experienced insiders as role models 0.44, investiture tactics 0.52 and on-the-job embeddedness 0.42 for turnover within a year [155](#cite:155).

short: k is the number of studies and N the total sample behind a meta-analytic estimate; the guide quotes both with every effect size, as reported.
definition: In a meta-analytic result k is the number of studies or samples pooled and N the total number of people across them, and the pack's evidence grade for a meta-analysis requires the effect size to be quoted with its k and N as reported (scope.yaml). The structured-interview databases behind the 2022 re-estimation are k = 36 with N = 3,069 and k = 69 with N = 4,795; job knowledge tests rest on k = 59 and N = 3,965, biodata on k = 49 and N = 20,564, work samples on k = 54 and N = 10,469 [1](#cite:1). The mechanical-versus-clinical comparison for job performance rests on k = 9 with N = 1,392 mechanical and 1,156 clinical, which is why its authors call the values probable underestimates [7](#cite:7). The lever records carry the pair in a field of their own.

short: A randomized or natural experiment in real hiring or employment settings; the guide's second evidence grade.
definition: A field experiment, in the pack's evidence grades, is a randomized or natural experiment in real hiring or employment settings (scope.yaml). The pack's examples include a randomized trial in which 48 computer-science students solved the same problem watched or in private [21](#cite:21); a natural field experiment in which nearly 2,500 job seekers were randomly assigned to job ads with and without a statement that wages were negotiable [95](#cite:95); university employees randomly informed of a public salary database [92](#cite:92); and a discrete-choice experiment with job seekers in a national call center's hiring process [115](#cite:115). One small trial with students leaves the effect size in working engineers unknown, which is why the lever built on it says so [21](#cite:21).

short: Difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity or matched designs on administrative or firm data; the guide's third evidence grade.
definition: A quasi-experimental design, in the pack's evidence grades, is a difference-in-differences, regression-discontinuity or matched design on administrative or firm data, ranked below a field experiment and above observational research (scope.yaml). The pack's examples use the staggered introduction of a job test across fifteen service-sector firms [10](#cite:10); a national retailer whose 1,363 stores switched from informal to test-based screening within one year [11](#cite:11); the hiring records of nine large firms on referrals [60](#cite:60); and state-by-state adoption of pay-range posting laws [97](#cite:97).

short: A quasi-experimental design that compares states that adopted a law with states that did not, before and after; the guide's pay-transparency and salary-history evidence uses it.
definition: Difference-in-differences is the first of the designs the pack's quasi-experimental grade names (scope.yaml), and two of the pack's law-effect studies use it, with the comparison running between states that adopted a law and states that did not [97](#cite:97) [96](#cite:96). The study of state pay-range posting laws, a difference-in-differences across three datasets, found disclosure in postings rose about 30 percentage points and wages rose 1.3 to 3.6 percent with no effect on employment, posting volume or dispersion [97](#cite:97). The study of early salary-history bans, using difference-in-differences and synthetic control, found the gender earnings ratio rose about 1 percent in states with bans, driven by recent job changers and workers over 35 [96](#cite:96).

short: A survey of HR professionals or employers by an association or vendor; carried for benchmark facts only, with publisher and year named, never as evidence of a lever's effect.
definition: A practitioner survey, in the pack's evidence grades, is a survey by SHRM or a similar association or vendor, carried for benchmark facts only with the publisher and year named (scope.yaml); a vendor case study is never evidence of a lever's effect. The grade covers the 2025 SHRM benchmarks of more than 2,300 members (a median time to fill of about 45 days; 41 percent citing rising ghosting) [43](#cite:43) and the 2,371-member benchmarking brief behind the cost-per-hire medians [196](#cite:196); the hidden-workers employer survey in which 88 percent of employers reported exact-match rejections of qualified high-skilled candidates [44](#cite:44); a staffing firm's survey of more than 5,500 managers on counteroffers [113](#cite:113); and the survey of 959 HR professionals that measured the research–practice gap in beliefs about selection [20](#cite:20).

short: The label on every lever, constraint and link saying what kind of evidence stands behind it, from meta-analysis down to synthesis; defined on the methods page.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
The evidence grade is the label every lever, constraint and dependency link carries to say what kind of evidence stands behind it. The grades, defined in scope.yaml and shown on the methods page, run from meta-analysis (a published meta-analysis or systematic review, quoted with its k and N) through field experiment (a randomized or natural experiment in a real employment setting), quasi-experimental (difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity or matched designs on administrative or firm data), observational (survey research without a causal design) and practitioner survey (benchmark facts only, publisher and year named), to regulation (statute, CFR, FAR, executive order or directive, which binds regardless of evidence), guidance (an agency's or standards body's recommended practice, not binding) and synthesis (a conclusion no cited work states on its own). A constraint carries the strongest grade among its sources, a lever the grade of the evidence for its effect, and a link the strongest grade on the edge.

short: The guide's label for a conclusion no cited work states on its own; the lowest evidence grade, marked visibly wherever it appears.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
Synthesis is the guide's label for a conclusion that no cited work states on its own: a step from evidence to a dependency link, a diagnostic a recruiter can run that no source supplies, or an inference across sources. It is the lowest evidence grade in scope.yaml, it is marked visibly in the app and listed on the methods page, and in the record files it appears as the word synthesis in parentheses after the sentence it qualifies, with the citations the inference rests on still attached. In the prose chapters the marker is a comment line before the paragraph. The rule exists so that a reader can tell what a study found from what the guide's author concluded.

short: The record of the author's original staffing matrix, every row and category carried as a hypothesis and adjudicated against the evidence; never a source of fact.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
The hypothesis ledger is hypotheses.yaml, the record of the author's own starting point: a private staffing trade-off matrix of sixty rows in eight categories, supplied before the sweeps began and described by the author as best guesses needing more rigor. Every row, every category and each of the seven original failure patterns is carried as a hypothesis, never as a source of fact, with firm-specific wording removed. Each sweep adjudicated the entries it touched and gave each a status from a fixed vocabulary: supported, partly supported, contradicted, unstudied (searched, nothing found either way), reframed (the category dissolved into other records) or untested; each entry names the records that absorbed it and carries one or two cited sentences of evidence. The ledger closed after the plan sweep with no entry untested, and it renders on the methods page.

short: One of the eight observed failure points in patterns.yaml, written as a recruiter sees it; the pathfinder's first question, pointing at the constraints that explain it.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
A failure pattern is one of the eight observed failure points in patterns.yaml, written in the words a recruiter would use: many applicants but few who qualify; candidates who withdraw before a decision; few plausible candidates; candidates who pass but decline; candidates who accept but cannot start; employees who start but struggle; productive employees who leave; and a candidate the firm approves and the customer rejects. Each pattern belongs to a stage, carries a cited account of what the evidence says usually underlies it, points at the constraints that explain it with a cited reason for each, and names the ledger hypothesis it tests. The pattern is the pathfinder's first question, because a recruiter sees the symptom before the cause.

short: A record of something that binds an opening at one stage: what it is, why it happens, how to tell, which levers and gates apply, who decides, and its evidence grade.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
A constraint is a record in constraints.yaml describing something that binds an opening at one of the nine stages, replacing the rows of the original matrix with evidence-backed entries. Each carries a plain account of what the constraint is, the mechanism as the literature or the regulation explains it, diagnostics a recruiter can run (how to tell), the indicators shown in its panel, the levers that act on it, the gates that apply, the pathfinder situations it matches, who decides the outcome (the firm, the customer or the contract, the law, the market or the candidate), its evidence grade, any controversy it sits inside, and the ledger hypotheses it tests. Every sentence of fact in it is cited, and a diagnostic without a source is marked synthesis. Constraints are the nodes of the dependency graph.

short: A record of something the firm can do about a constraint, with its evidence grade, the effect exactly as reported, what it does not do, its costs and the constraints it can worsen.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
A lever is a record in levers.yaml describing something the firm can do about a constraint, replacing the original matrix's suggested mitigations and trade-offs. Each carries what the lever is, an evidence block with its grade, the effect exactly as reported, the population and the k and N, a statement of what the lever does not do, its costs as reported, the constraints it can worsen elsewhere (each drawn as a dependency link), the gates and enablers that apply, how-to steps taken from a cited guidance source and never invented, and the ledger hypotheses it tests. Nothing in a lever is a recommendation; the record says what a cited study found a practice did, in which population, and what it did not do.

short: A record of a regulatory or contractual rule that binds an opening regardless of evidence, with its governing text, thresholds, steps and pending changes.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
A gate is a record in gates.yaml for a regulatory or contractual rule that binds an opening regardless of evidence: a statute, a regulation, a FAR or DFARS clause, an executive order, an agency directive or a contract term. Each carries a cited account of what the rule requires, the governing text, when it applies (with thresholds), the stages it binds, the steps it imposes, the official URL, any pending changes with a status from a fixed vocabulary (proposed, announced, class deviation, final, pending implementation, suspended or withdrawn), and a conflicts line that says when the record rests on a law-firm or vendor summary instead of the primary text. The state overlays in states.yaml modify the federal gates state by state.

short: A record of a public data source, program, reference, standard or tooling category a recruiter can put to work, recorded as its owner states it; no vendor is recommended.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
An enabler is a record in enablers.yaml for a public data source, a government program, a reference document, a standard or a category of tooling that a recruiter without an HR department can put to work, recorded as its owner states it. Each carries what the enabler does, its cost, its conditions, the levers it supports, the official URL and any pending changes. Tooling records name a category and list examples by the vendors' own descriptions; no vendor is recommended and no fee appears except as a fact with a source.

short: A record of a headline figure with its reference period, publication date, publisher and series; never timeless, shown in the node panels of the constraints that cite it.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
An indicator is a record in indicators.yaml for a headline figure with its date: a value, the reference period it describes, the publication date, the publisher, the series identifier for the refresh routine where one exists, the stages it belongs to and the sources behind it. The file's rule is that no indicator is timeless: a median time to fill, a clearance processing time, a job openings rate or a cost-per-hire median is shown with the period it measures and the date it was published, and a figure for which no newer count exists stands at its last date and says so. Indicators appear in the node panels of the constraints that cite them.

short: An edge in links.yaml between two records, with a relation (precondition, amplifies, trade-off, enables), a short label and its own cited evidence; the graph draws exactly these.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
A dependency link is an edge in links.yaml between two records, drawn exactly as written and never inferred by the app. Each carries a tail and a head, a relation from a fixed vocabulary (precondition, meaning the head cannot be addressed until the tail is; amplifies, meaning the tail makes the head worse; trade-off, meaning acting on the tail worsens the head; enables, meaning acting on the tail makes the head easier), a label of at most twelve words drawn on the arrow, one to three cited sentences of evidence for the dependency, the strongest evidence grade on the edge, and the ledger hypothesis it tests. The step from evidence to edge is marked synthesis where the cited works do not state it. The graph's walks of what a record depends on, and what depends on it, follow these edges and nothing else.

short: The app's deterministic narrowing page: failure pattern, stage, role conditions and state, scored and ranked, never recommended, then passed to the graph as the highlighted set.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
The pathfinder is the app's deterministic narrowing page. It asks four questions: the observed failure pattern (one answer), the stage if known (one), the conditions of the role (several: requires a clearance, the customer approves the candidate, a developmental hire is possible, onsite with a fixed schedule, a rare skill or passive market, pay above the rate, tight cash or budget, an urgent start, a tentative opening, an overloaded team), and the state of work (one, selecting the state overlay). Each record scores three points for matching the pattern, two for the stage and one for each condition; records scoring zero are hidden; the page shows why each record matched; nothing is recommended, only ranked. The narrowed field is passed to the dependency graph as the highlighted set.

short: The browser-local notepad for one opening: pinned constraints, chosen levers, owner, decision date and measure; exported as Markdown or JSON, never leaving the browser.
definition:
<!-- framing -->
A decision record is the browser-local notepad the app keeps for one opening: the primary and secondary constraints the recruiter pinned, the levers chosen, the owner, the decision date and the measure by which the decision will be judged. It can be exported as Markdown or JSON and never leaves the browser, so nothing a recruiter writes about a real opening reaches the guide or anyone else.

short: A computational tool that makes or supports an employment decision; New York City, California and Colorado define and regulate it under different names (AEDT, ADS, ADMT).
definition: An automated employment decision tool is New York City's term, under Local Law 144, for a tool an employer may use only after a bias audit no more than a year old, with a published summary and candidate notice, on penalties of \$500 to \$1,500 a day; in two years the enforcement agency received two complaints, and its review of 32 companies found one issue where the state auditors found at least 17 potential instances of non-compliance [37](#cite:37). California's regulations, effective October 1, 2025, call it an automated-decision system, any computational process that makes or supports an employment decision, extend liability to agents, treat anti-bias testing before and after adoption as a defense factor and require four-year retention of ADS records [40](#cite:40). Colorado's replacement act calls it automated decision-making technology and, from January 1, 2027, requires notice before it materially influences an employment decision, an explanation within 30 days of an adverse outcome, human review and three-year records [222](#cite:222). Federally, such a tool is a selection procedure under the Uniform Guidelines [35](#cite:35).

short: Using software, an algorithm or AI to screen, rank, score or interview candidates; a selection procedure under the Uniform Guidelines, with state notice, audit and retention duties on top.
definition: Algorithmic screening is the use of software, an algorithm or AI to screen, rank, score or interview candidates. The EEOC's technical assistance of May 18, 2023, removed from its website on January 27, 2025 without any change in the underlying law, stated that such a tool used to make or inform a selection decision is a selection procedure under the Uniform Guidelines, that the employer can be liable for a vendor's tool, and that the four-fifths rule is a rule of thumb [35](#cite:35) [36](#cite:36). States now carry the duties: Illinois bars discriminatory AI use and requires notice from January 1, 2026 [38](#cite:38), New York City requires an annual bias audit [37](#cite:37), and California's regulations require anti-bias testing and four-year records [40](#cite:40). A screen can be built to add validity while reducing subgroup differences, as NLP scoring of narrative applications did across four samples (N = 1,828), predicting board scores at r of about .60 [23](#cite:23). Exact-match résumé filters are the other face of the same constraint: 88 percent of employers in one survey said qualified high-skilled candidates were rejected outright for not matching criteria exactly [44](#cite:44).

short: A neutral selection procedure that disproportionately excludes a protected group; lawful only if job-related and consistent with business necessity, and open to a less discriminatory alternative.
definition: Disparate impact, as the EEOC's fact sheet of December 1, 2007 maps it, is a neutral procedure that disproportionately excludes a protected group; the employer must then show the procedure is job-related and consistent with business necessity, and the challenger may show a less discriminatory alternative [33](#cite:33). Disparate treatment is the intentional kind, and the ADEA permits neutral practices affecting workers 40 and older only on a reasonable factor other than age [33](#cite:33). The Uniform Guidelines supply the evidentiary test, the four-fifths rule of thumb and the validation standards [31](#cite:31) [32](#cite:32); a criminal-record policy that disproportionately screens out a protected group is judged the same way, with arrest-only exclusions generally not job-related [47](#cite:47). The state AI statutes add notice, audit and retention duties without changing the Title VII test [35](#cite:35) [40](#cite:40).

short: A question asked of applicants before a conditional offer; the ADA, the Fair Chance Act, the citizenship-status rule and the salary-history bans each reserve or restrict particular questions.
definition: A pre-employment inquiry is what the law lets an employer ask before a conditional offer, and four rules bind it. Under the ADA, disability-related questions, defined as questions likely to elicit information about a disability, and medical examinations are barred before a conditional offer, while questions about the ability to perform job functions with or without accommodation, licenses, attendance and arrest or conviction records are allowed; after the offer, medical inquiries are allowed if required of everyone entering the job category [34](#cite:34). Under the federal Fair Chance Act a contractor may not ask about criminal history for positions under a federal contract until after a conditional offer, with exceptions for classified-access and national-security positions [48](#cite:48). Under 8 U.S.C. 1324b a posting for export-controlled work may not be limited to U.S. citizens, or to citizens and permanent residents [49](#cite:49) [51](#cite:51). About twenty states bar questions about prior pay [106](#cite:106). The constraint is `c-premature-inquiries`.

variants: Fair Chance to Compete for Jobs Act
short: The federal Fair Chance to Compete for Jobs Act: since December 20, 2021 a contractor may not ask about criminal history for positions under a federal contract until after a conditional offer.
definition: The Fair Chance Act, enacted in the FY2020 National Defense Authorization Act of December 20, 2019 and effective for contractors and agencies on December 20, 2021, bars a federal contractor from asking about or seeking an applicant's criminal history for positions within the scope of a federal contract until after a conditional offer [48](#cite:48). Exceptions cover positions with law-enforcement or national-security duties, positions requiring access to classified information and positions where a law requires the inquiry earlier, so most cleared work is exempt; a first violation brings a notice and warning and later violations can suspend payments under the contract [48](#cite:48). Only a law-firm summary was read, so the implementing FAR clause is a todo on the gate `fair-chance-act-contractors` [48](#cite:48). The EEOC's separate guidance governs how a record, once known, may be used: a targeted screen with individualized assessment [47](#cite:47).

short: State and local fair-chance laws that take the criminal-history question off the application or delay it to an interview or a conditional offer; fifteen states cover private employers.
definition: Ban the box is the name for state and local fair-chance hiring laws that take the criminal-history question off the application or delay it. The compilation the pack relies on lists thirty-seven states with a policy, fifteen of which cover private employers, with timing that ranges from keeping the question off the application to after the first interview (New Jersey, Oregon and Rhode Island) and after a conditional offer (California and Hawaii), plus Louisiana's 2021 private-employer law without a timing rule [216](#cite:216); a 2026 vendor list confirms the same private-employer states and names eleven states with no statewide law, two of which preempt local rules [217](#cite:217). The pack carries the overlay for every state in states.yaml as compilation-sourced with the statutes pending, and the federal Fair Chance Act applies to contract positions in every state [216](#cite:216) [48](#cite:48).

short: A contract-defined class of labor under a time-and-materials or labor-hour contract, with its own fixed hourly rate and its own qualifications.
definition: Under a time-and-materials or labor-hour contract the hourly rate is the contract rate for labor meeting the qualifications of a specified labor category, and that rate includes wages, overhead, G&A and profit [98](#cite:98). Hours performed by employees who do not meet the category's qualifications are not paid unless the contracting officer authorizes it, and vouchers must be supported by records showing qualifications [99](#cite:99). Where the contract was not competitively awarded, separate rates apply to the contractor, each subcontractor and each affiliate [98](#cite:98). The offer stage treats the category rate as a ceiling the firm did not set, and the pack's records derive the affordable salary from it as a synthesis [98](#cite:98).

short: The education and experience line a contract attaches to a labor category; only labor that meets it can be billed at the category rate.
definition: The qualifications are the terms in the contract that decide who may be billed against a labor category: hours worked by employees who do not meet them are not paid to the extent of that work unless the contracting officer authorizes it, and the contractor keeps records showing qualifications to support its vouchers [99](#cite:99). One audit of twelve task orders found the government improperly charged for 101 of 112 employees who did not meet the labor-category requirements, and that contracting officers had not validated 1,219 of 1,287 qualifications through résumé review [173](#cite:173). The plan-stage records call the category line the one enforceable definition of "qualified" among the three a customer-governed requisition mixes together [99](#cite:99) [197](#cite:197).

short: A contract type that pays fixed hourly rates per labor category, under a ceiling price, for work whose extent or duration could not be estimated at award.
definition: A time-and-materials contract pays fixed hourly rates per labor category that include wages, overhead, general and administrative expense and profit, requires a ceiling price, and is used only when the extent or duration of the work cannot be estimated accurately when the contract is placed [98](#cite:98). Its payment clause pays labor hours only for employees who meet the category's qualifications unless the contracting officer authorizes otherwise, and permits a 5 percent reserve of up to \$50,000 [99](#cite:99). A labor-hour contract is paid under the same clause [99](#cite:99). The rate fixed at award moves only through the contract's adjustment clause, which on GSA schedules allows at most three increases per contract period [117](#cite:117).

short: The multiplier that turns a salary into a billing rate by loading fringe, overhead, G&A and profit; the pack marks the arithmetic as synthesis.
definition: A billing rate is built in layers: fringe benefits allocated on labor, overhead applied to direct labor and fringe, general and administrative expense applied to total cost input, and profit entered as a rate [206](#cite:206). Read the other way, the labor-category rate already contains the wage, the indirect costs and the profit, so the affordable salary is what remains after the firm's indirect rates and margin are subtracted; the pack marks that wrap-rate arithmetic as a synthesis from the regulation [98](#cite:98). The plan-stage lever `l-wrap-rate-feasibility-check` applies the layers to market pay for the category and compares the result with the contract rate or the schedule ceiling before a posting goes out [206](#cite:206) [98](#cite:98) [111](#cite:111).

short: The first layer of a billing rate: fringe benefit cost expressed as a rate on direct labor.
definition: In the rate structure a government cost proposal assumes, fringe benefits are allocated on labor, and overhead is then applied to direct labor and fringe together [206](#cite:206). The layer is real money: benefits were 30.0 percent of private-industry compensation cost in June 2026 and 31.5 percent for management, professional and related occupations [104](#cite:104). On a Service Contract Act contract the fringe floor for covered service employees is the health-and-welfare rate in the wage determination, \$5.55 per hour from July 2025 [101](#cite:101).

short: The second layer of a billing rate: indirect cost applied to direct labor plus fringe.
definition: Overhead is applied to direct labor and fringe in the rate build-up a government cost proposal assumes, before general and administrative expense is applied to total cost input and profit is added as a rate [206](#cite:206). Indirect costs are those remaining to be allocated to intermediate or two or more final cost objectives, accumulated in logical groupings with an allocation base common to all of them, over the cost accounting period [148](#cite:148). Payroll that cannot be charged to a contract, such as a hire waiting for a clearance, is an indirect cost pooled and spread over the firm's other work through its rates [148](#cite:148).

short: The G&A layer of a billing rate: general and administrative expense applied to total cost input, after fringe and overhead.
definition: General and administrative expense is applied to total cost input in the rate structure a government cost proposal assumes, after fringe on labor and overhead on labor and fringe, with profit entered as a rate on top [206](#cite:206). The T&M regulation names G&A, with wages, overhead and profit, as a component of every labor-category hourly rate [98](#cite:98). Like overhead, it is an indirect cost accumulated in a logical grouping and allocated on a common base over the cost accounting period [148](#cite:148).

short: The profit element of a billing rate, entered as a rate on top of fringe, overhead and G&A; the pack's offer records call it fee.
definition: Profit is entered as a rate on top of fringe, overhead and general and administrative expense in the build-up a government cost proposal assumes [206](#cite:206), and the T&M regulation includes profit in every labor-category hourly rate [98](#cite:98). The offer-stage lever `l-set-range-from-rate-and-market` subtracts fringe, overhead, G&A and fee at the firm's own rates from the category rate to find the affordable salary, a step the pack marks as synthesis [98](#cite:98). The word has a second sense in the plan-stage records, where agency fees are one component of the cost of a hire in the SHRM benchmark [196](#cite:196).

short: The government audit agency the rate build-up names as an approver of a contractor's indirect rates.
definition: The pack carries the agency in one role: a government cost proposal uses indirect rates approved by a government agency such as the Defense Contract Audit Agency within the past 30 months, and an offeror without approved rates provides the detailed costs and calculations behind its own [206](#cite:206). The rates in question are the fringe, overhead, G&A and profit layers between a salary and a billing rate [206](#cite:206). No other record in the pack describes the agency's audits of labor-category billing; the one enforcement example carried is an inspector-general audit of task orders [173](#cite:173).

short: The OFPP benchmark above which compensation is unallowable on covered contracts: $671,000 for 2025 by an accounting firm's figure.
definition: Compensation above the benchmark set by OFPP under 41 U.S.C. 1127 is unallowable for all employees on awards from June 24, 2014, with narrow exceptions possible for scientists and engineers [100](#cite:100). The benchmark was \$646,000 for 2024 and \$671,000 for 2025, set as the prior cap times the change in the Employment Cost Index, with \$695,000 estimated for 2026; the figures rest on an accounting firm's page because the OFPP determination was not found, and the gate record flags that [107](#cite:107). The offer-stage record notes that the cap does not bind technical hires at a small firm's pay levels [107](#cite:107).

short: A cost the government will reimburse or recognize in rates under the FAR Part 31 cost principles; an unallowable cost stays with the firm.
definition: Under the compensation cost principle, pay is allowable when it is reasonable for the work and conforms to an established plan or consistent practice, with reasonableness judged against firms of similar size, industry and area doing similar non-government work; bonuses are allowable only under an agreement or plan established before the services [100](#cite:100). Training and education related to the field in which the employee works are allowable, while training for other than bona fide employees is not [175](#cite:175). Indirect costs are accumulated by logical cost groupings and allocated over a common base [148](#cite:148). Consent to a subcontract does not make any cost allowable [199](#cite:199).

short: The FAR cost principle on compensation for personal services: reasonableness, an established plan, the bonus rule and the compensation cap.
definition: FAR 31.205-6 governs what a cost-type contractor can recover in pay: compensation must be reasonable for the work and conform to an established plan or consistent practice; no presumption of allowability attaches to major plan changes made without the administrative contracting officer's chance to review; bonuses are allowable only under a pre-existing agreement or plan; severance and pension supplements are limited; and compensation above the OFPP benchmark is unallowable for all employees on awards from June 24, 2014 [100](#cite:100). The gate record `far-31-205-6-compensation-allowability` binds the offer and retain stages and carries the cap figure from an accounting firm pending the OFPP primary [100](#cite:100) [107](#cite:107).

short: The federal statute that sets locally prevailing wages and fringe benefits, through wage determinations, on service contracts over $2,500.
definition: The McNamara-O'Hara Service Contract Act requires federal service contracts over \$2,500 whose principal purpose is services by service employees to pay the locally prevailing wages and fringe benefits in the wage determination attached to the contract, generally drawn from BLS OEWS data, plus vacation and holiday pay, and it sets the health-and-welfare rate [101](#cite:101). The higher contractor minimum wage under EO 14026 was revoked by EO 14236 on March 14, 2025 and is no longer enforced; EO 13658 remains for contracts entered or renewed between January 1, 2015 and January 29, 2022, at \$13.65 from May 11, 2026 [102](#cite:102) [101](#cite:101). The Act's floors still attach to a successor contract after the nondisplacement order's revocation [101](#cite:101) [186](#cite:186).

short: The schedule of prevailing wage and fringe rates, by locality and occupation, attached to a Service Contract Act contract as a floor.
definition: A wage determination lists the locally prevailing wages and fringe benefits a service contractor must pay its covered service employees, generally drawn from BLS OEWS data, with the health-and-welfare rate on top; determinations are published by locality on SAM.gov, and unlisted classifications are conformed [101](#cite:101). The gate record reads the listed rate and the H&W amount as floors beneath the labor-category rate, which is the ceiling [101](#cite:101) [98](#cite:98). Those floors move on the Department of Labor's calendar, which is one reason a contract rate fixed at award can lag the market [101](#cite:101) [103](#cite:103).

short: The Service Contract Act fringe benefit rate per hour: $5.55 from July 2025, $5.09 where EO 13706 applies, and $2.42 or $1.96 in Hawaii.
definition: The health-and-welfare rate is the fixed fringe benefit amount a Service Contract Act wage determination carries on top of the prevailing wage: \$5.55 per hour from July 2025, \$5.09 where EO 13706 also applies, and \$2.42 or \$1.96 in Hawaii [101](#cite:101). The changes file records the July 2025 rate as `ch-012`, and the indicator `ind-sca-health-welfare-2025` carries it for the offer and plan stages [101](#cite:101). The offer-stage constraint `c-contract-rates-lag-market` lists the rate among the floors that move on the Department of Labor's calendar and not the firm's [101](#cite:101).

short: A contract clause naming individuals essential to performance who cannot be diverted or replaced without the contracting officer's written consent.
definition: Where a contract names key personnel, they are considered essential to work performance and cannot be diverted, replaced or announced as changed without the contracting officer's written consent; the HHS clause carried as the example requires at least 30 days' notice before a voluntary move, with a justification and a replacement whose skills, experience and credentials meet or exceed the contract's requirements, and the maximum practicable notice when a person is terminated for cause or leaves on less than 30 days [188](#cite:188). The FAR has no government-wide key-personnel clause, and other agencies' clauses set their own periods and standards [188](#cite:188). Before award, the people a proposal names are governed by the availability rule and the bait-and-switch standard [108](#cite:108) [203](#cite:203).

short: Replacing a named key person under the contract's clause: written consent, notice and a substitute who meets or exceeds the requirement.
definition: Under the clause carried as the example, a voluntary diversion of a named key person needs at least 30 days' notice to the contracting officer with a justification and a replacement request showing skills, experience and credentials that meet or exceed the contract's requirements, and the contract is modified to add or delete key personnel [188](#cite:188). The clause gives the contractor the notice period and the government no period to answer, which the plan-stage record `c-customer-approval-cycle` treats as a clock the candidate experiences [188](#cite:188). The handover records tie the substitution to the backfill: an internal move off a named position needs the customer's consent and an equal-or-better substitute first [188](#cite:188).

short: GAO's rule that an offeror who knows a proposed key person has become unavailable before award must tell the agency; the Court of Federal Claims reads the duty more narrowly.
definition: At GAO an offeror with actual knowledge that a proposed key person has become unavailable before award must notify the agency, which then either rejects the proposal as unacceptable or reopens discussions; the Orion decision of December 30, 2024 applied the duty to protesters as well as awardees [108](#cite:108). The Court of Federal Claims declined to impose that duty absent a solicitation provision, statute or regulation, requiring only a reasonable belief at submission that the proposed personnel would be available [109](#cite:109). Declarations of continued availability have defeated dismissal motions [114](#cite:114). The gate record flags the conflict between the two forums and reads the solicitation's own notice terms as controlling [108](#cite:108) [109](#cite:109).

short: GAO's protest standard for a proposal that knowingly or negligently relies on personnel the firm has no reasonable basis to furnish.
definition: A bait-and-switch protest succeeds where the awardee knowingly or negligently represented that it would rely on specific personnel it lacked a reasonable basis to furnish, the agency relied on the representation, and the reliance had a material effect on the evaluation [203](#cite:203). GAO sustained such a protest in December 2022 where a proposed key person had told the awardee she had committed to the protester and could not be used, the quotation still carried her résumé, the agency credited it with a strength, and an 18.5 percent price premium rested on it; the remedy was exclusion, termination and a new selection [203](#cite:203). The gate `proposal-staffing-representations` pairs the standard with GAO's duty to report a key person who becomes unavailable [203](#cite:203) [108](#cite:108).

short: A contract characterized by an employer-employee relationship between the government and the contractor's staff; barred unless a statute authorizes it.
definition: A personal services contract is one characterized by the employer-employee relationship it creates between the government and the contractor's personnel, and agencies may not award one unless a statute specifically authorizes it [197](#cite:197). The relationship arises when contractor personnel are subject to the relatively continuous supervision and control of a government officer or employee; giving orders for a specific result, with the right to reject the product, does not by itself create it [197](#cite:197). The rule's descriptive elements are performance on site, government-furnished tools, services applied to the agency's integral effort, comparable civil-service work, a need lasting beyond a year and a nature requiring government direction [197](#cite:197). FAR Case 2026-002, proposed June 23, 2026, would reorganize Part 37 with no stated change of policy, so the rule's citation may move [228](#cite:228).

short: A FAR category of work the pack carries only by its location: the overhaul rulemaking moves it from subpart 7.5 to subpart 37.3.
definition: The pack carries the term only in the FAR overhaul's rulemaking: the proposed rule for FAR Case 2026-002, published June 23, 2026, would move inherently governmental functions from subpart 7.5 to subpart 37.3 as part of a rewrite of Part 37 that states no substantive change of policy [228](#cite:228). The same proposed rule places the personal-services prohibition in a reorganized Part 37, so both citations may move even if the rules do not [228](#cite:228) [227](#cite:227). No record in the pack defines the category or applies it to staffing.

short: FAR 52.219-14: on a set-aside services contract, no more than 50 percent of the amount paid may go to subcontractors that are not similarly situated.
definition: On a small business set-aside or sole-source services contract, the prime will not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the government for contract performance to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities; the limit is 50 percent for supplies excluding materials, 85 percent for general construction and 75 percent for special trade construction [198](#cite:198). A similarly situated entity is a first-tier subcontractor with the same small business program status that is small under the subcontract's NAICS code, and its own further subcontracting counts against the cap; compliance is measured by the end of the base term and each option period, or of each order [198](#cite:198). The plan-stage record `c-partner-support-limits` reads the clause as one of three bounds on filling a gap with a partner's people [198](#cite:198) [199](#cite:199) [187](#cite:187).

short: FAR 52.244-2: without an approved purchasing system, the contracting officer's advance consent is needed before a cost-type, T&M or labor-hour subcontract.
definition: A contractor without an approved purchasing system needs the contracting officer's advance consent for any cost-reimbursement, time-and-materials or labor-hour subcontract and for fixed-price subcontracts above a threshold, with notice describing the supplies or services, the type, the proposed subcontractor and the price; consent does not relieve the contractor of responsibility for performance or make any cost allowable [199](#cite:199). A subcontract is any contract a subcontractor enters to furnish supplies or services for performance of the prime contract [199](#cite:199). The plan-stage lever `l-customer-approved-partner-support` requires the consent before a partner's people start [199](#cite:199).

short: An agreement between firms to pursue or perform work together; its hiring and pay terms fall under the DOJ/FTC worker guidelines.
definition: The pack treats teaming through its hiring terms. The DOJ and FTC guidelines of January 2025 apply to employers collaborating in joint ventures and teaming arrangements: agreements not to recruit, solicit or hire each other's workers are illegal even without actual harm, while a no-hire or no-solicit term that is subordinate and collateral to a legitimate collaboration and reasonably necessary to it receives a fuller effects analysis [187](#cite:187). The gate `no-poach-and-non-solicitation` applies to any teaming, subcontract or prime relationship with hiring or pay terms, and the lever `l-lawful-non-solicitation-terms` scopes any non-solicit term to the collaboration and its duration [187](#cite:187). Partner support on a set-aside is also bounded by the subcontracting limit and the consent requirement [198](#cite:198) [199](#cite:199).

short: An agreement between employers not to recruit, solicit or hire each other's workers; illegal under the 2025 DOJ/FTC guidelines and prosecutable as a felony.
