definition: Under the DOJ and FTC antitrust guidelines of January 2025, agreements between competing employers not to recruit, solicit or hire each other's workers are illegal even without actual harm and may be prosecuted as felonies; the guidelines replace the 2016 guidance for human resource professionals [187](#cite:187). Agreements to align or coordinate compensation, even a starting point, are wage-fixing, and exchanging competitively sensitive compensation information, including through third parties or algorithms, may be unlawful [187](#cite:187). The retain-stage record `c-poaching-by-prime-or-customer` concludes that restrictions on the hiring party are criminal and restrictions on the person are state-limited, so the hold has to be in the job [187](#cite:187) [169](#cite:169) [178](#cite:178).

short: A term barring solicitation of a firm's workers or customers; it survives antitrust review only as a collateral, necessary part of a real collaboration.
definition: Under the 2025 DOJ and FTC guidelines, a no-hire or no-solicit term gets an effects analysis only when it is subordinate and collateral to a legitimate collaboration and reasonably necessary to it; a bare agreement between competing employers not to solicit each other's workers is illegal without any showing of harm [187](#cite:187). Washington's ESHB 1155, effective June 30, 2027, voids every noncompetition covenant but keeps nonsolicitation agreements, with the customer restriction capped at 18 months [210](#cite:210). The retain-stage lever `l-lawful-non-solicitation-terms` keeps any non-solicit term in a teaming or subcontract agreement scoped to the collaboration and its duration [187](#cite:187).

short: A covenant restricting a worker's later employment; a state-law question since the FTC acceded to the vacatur of its 2024 rule on September 5, 2025.
definition: The 2024 federal rule banning most noncompetes was held beyond the Commission's authority by a district court, and on September 5, 2025 the FTC voted 3–1 to dismiss its appeals and accede to the vacatur, leaving noncompetes to state law and case-by-case enforcement [169](#cite:169). The state map carried in `states.yaml` rests on a vendor tracker: statutory bans in six states, thirteen threshold or category regimes, and common-law reasonableness elsewhere, as of July 22, 2026 [209](#cite:209). Two 2026 changes are recorded: Tennessee's HB 1034 voids noncompetes for workers earning under \$70,000 from July 1, 2026 [209](#cite:209), and Washington's ESHB 1155 makes every noncompetition covenant void from June 30, 2027 regardless of signing date, with notice to affected workers by October 1, 2027 [210](#cite:210). The develop-stage gate reads a noncompete on a trained and cleared engineer as a state question and a retention question [169](#cite:169).

short: Pay during a post-employment restriction; the pack carries the term only as the consideration Massachusetts's noncompete statute may require.
definition: The pack carries garden leave in one place: the noncompete tracker's Massachusetts entry, where the statute limits noncompetes to FLSA-exempt workers, generally for 12 months, and requires notice and garden-leave pay or other agreed consideration [209](#cite:209). The state record `us-ma` carries that entry with the statute pending, since the tracker is a vendor page [209](#cite:209). No other record defines the practice or reports evidence on it.

short: A term requiring a worker to repay training costs on leaving; nearly 10 percent of workers were covered in 2020, and states now bar or narrow such terms.
definition: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau treats training repayment agreement provisions as employer-driven debt: nearly 10 percent of American workers surveyed in 2020 were covered, the Bureau documented repayment demands far above training cost and interest it found usurious, and the research it cites puts a training contract's effect at around 15 percent less quitting [166](#cite:166). California bars, for contracts entered after January 1, 2026, terms requiring repayment of training, education, relocation, signing or retention amounts for leaving before a date, with exceptions for a transferable credential under a separate, at-cost, prorated agreement and for approved apprenticeships, and with a \$5,000 penalty or actual damages [167](#cite:167). Colorado allows repayment only for training distinct from normal on-the-job training, at reasonable cost declining proportionally over two years, with a \$5,000 per-worker penalty [168](#cite:168). The former NLRB general counsel's memoranda against such terms were rescinded, and the FTC rule that would have treated some of them as noncompetes never took effect [168](#cite:168) [169](#cite:169).

short: A term that makes a worker pay or forfeit something for leaving before a date; limited by statute in four states, with New York and Washington to follow in 2027.
definition: A stay-or-pay provision requires repayment of training, education, relocation, signing or retention amounts, or a penalty, when a worker leaves before a stated date; California's AB 692 makes such terms unlawful in contracts entered after January 1, 2026, excepting transferable credentials under a separate, prorated, at-cost agreement, signing bonuses with retention periods of two years or less and no interest, government loan programs and approved apprenticeships, with no repayment on a termination except for misconduct [167](#cite:167). The state overlay, drawn from law-firm maps with the statutes pending, lists general limits in California, New York, Connecticut, Colorado and Wyoming and healthcare-only limits in Indiana and Pennsylvania [211](#cite:211). New York's Trapped at Work Act takes effect February 13, 2027 [212](#cite:212), and Washington's ESHB 1155 treats repayment and forfeiture terms tied to working in one's field as void noncompetes from June 30, 2027, excepting educational-expense agreements that expire within 18 months [210](#cite:210).

short: A promise to repay the employer if employment ends before a stated time; barred in Connecticut since 1985 and unenforceable in New York from February 13, 2027.
definition: An employment promissory note is a repayment obligation that falls due if employment ends before a stated time; Connecticut has barred such notes as a condition of employment since 1985 for employers with 26 or more employees, excepting advances, property sales or leases, sabbatical obligations and collectively bargained terms [211](#cite:211) [168](#cite:168). New York's Trapped at Work Act, signed December 19, 2025 and amended February 13, 2026, makes employment promissory notes unenforceable from February 13, 2027, with exceptions for bonuses and relocation assistance unless termination was for a reason other than misconduct, tuition for a transferable credential under conditions, voluntary property sales or leases, sabbatical terms and collective agreements; fines run \$1,000 to \$5,000 per violation, with no private action [212](#cite:212). Both entries rest on law-firm summaries, and the gate flags the statutes as pending [212](#cite:212) [211](#cite:211).

short: The tax exclusion for up to $5,250 a year of employer-paid education or student-loan payments under a separate written plan; indexed after 2026.
definition: Up to \$5,250 per employee per calendar year of educational assistance is excludable from wages, with the amount adjusted for cost-of-living increases for taxable years beginning after 2026; it covers tuition, fees, books, supplies and equipment and, since March 27, 2020 and without an end date after the 2025 amendments, principal and interest on the employee's qualified education loans [174](#cite:174). The program must be a separate written plan for the exclusive benefit of employees, and employees must be told it exists and what its terms are [174](#cite:174). The develop-stage lever `l-training-with-lawful-retention-terms` pays for training under such a plan and expects the retention return mainly through who applies, since 80 percent of a tuition program's retention effect came through sorting in the one establishment studied [174](#cite:174) [160](#cite:160).

short: Training hours that count as hours worked for non-exempt employees unless all four FLSA conditions hold: outside hours, voluntary, not job related, no concurrent work.
definition: For non-exempt employees, attendance at lectures, meetings and training programs counts as working time unless all four conditions are met: it is outside normal hours, it is voluntary, it is not job related, and no other work is performed at the same time [170](#cite:170). The gate record `flsa-training-time` reads required onboarding, certification study the job needs and in-hours courses as paid time, a step it marks as synthesis from the fact sheet [170](#cite:170). Exempt professionals are outside the rule, but the cost of their training is still governed by the allowability rule for training and education [170](#cite:170) [175](#cite:175).

short: Paid work with related instruction and mentoring under standards registered with DOL or a state agency; about 940,000 participants in FY2024.
definition: A Registered Apprenticeship pairs paid work with related instruction and mentoring under standards registered with the Department of Labor or a state agency; the employer hub offers a standards builder and a partner finder, and a program can be approved for GI Bill benefits through a State Approving Agency [177](#cite:177). About 940,000 people participated in FY2024, computer occupations were the third-largest group at 7 percent, growth outside construction was 42 percent over four years, about 42 percent of participants complete within a year of the expected date, the median starting wage was \$19 an hour, and smaller employers told GAO that registration and reporting were especially hard and that cost deterred them [172](#cite:172). The federal cost-benefit study measured completers' career earnings gains of \$240,037 and social benefits exceeding costs by more than \$49,000, and nothing on the employer's side [171](#cite:171).

short: The DoD program that places transitioning service members with an industry partner in their last 180 days, on military pay, under an MOU with offer obligations.
definition: Under the DoD SkillBridge memorandum of understanding, transitioning service members train with an industry partner within 180 days of separation; the August 2024 MOU sets a minimum intake by employer size, one participant a year for employers of 200 or fewer, requires that at least 75 percent of completers receive a qualifying offer of immediate post-service employment with an 85 percent goal, and requires outcome and participation reporting at 90 and 180 days [74](#cite:74). The service continues the member's pay and benefits during the internship, as the law-firm summary states it [59](#cite:59). The MOU does not define a qualifying offer, no study of SkillBridge hiring outcomes was found, and the 75 percent figure is an obligation, not a result [74](#cite:74).

variants: Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act
short: The federal law requiring employers of 100 or more to give 60 days' written notice before a plant closing or mass layoff affecting 50 or more at one site.
definition: Employers with 100 or more employees, not counting those with under six months' service or under 20 hours a week, must give at least 60 calendar days' written notice before a plant closing or mass layoff affecting 50 or more employees at a single site, with exceptions for unforeseeable business circumstances, faltering companies and natural disasters [191](#cite:191). The gate record reads a contract loss at a site as a possible trigger for a firm above the threshold and notes, as synthesis, that most small firms are below it and owe only what state law and their own promises require [191](#cite:191). Fifteen states are reported to have mini-WARN laws, most with lower thresholds, and Washington amended its 2025 act by ESB 6106 on March 17, 2026 [213](#cite:213) [215](#cite:215).

short: A state layoff-notice law with its own thresholds; fifteen states are reported to have one, most below the federal 100-employee line.
definition: A mini-WARN law is a state counterpart to the federal notice act with its own employer threshold, trigger and notice period; a December 2025 law-firm alert names fifteen states with such laws, Ohio and Washington added in 2025, and the thresholds in the state overlay come from a 2024 benefits-broker chart without statute citations, so every row but Washington's is flagged primary-pending [213](#cite:213) [214](#cite:214). The chart's thresholds run from 25 employees with 30 days' notice in Iowa to 100 employees with 90 days' notice in Maine and in New Jersey, where severance is added [214](#cite:214). Washington's statute, ESB 6106 of 2026, covers employers with 50 or more employees in the state, requires 60 days' written notice to the Employment Security Department and each affected employee, and triggers on employment loss for 50 or more within any 30-day period [215](#cite:215). The Ohio entry could not be confirmed against a statute [213](#cite:213).

short: The federal default that a proper invoice is paid 30 days after receipt, with improper invoices returned within 7 days and interest paid automatically on late payment.
definition: Where the contract sets no date, payment is due 30 days after the start of the payment period, which begins on receipt of a proper invoice; an improper invoice is returned within 7 days, and interest is paid automatically on late payments [202](#cite:202). The plan-stage records treat the 30-day default as the cash gap a hire made ahead of the first invoice has to bridge, with payroll before billing sitting in the indirect pools [202](#cite:202) [148](#cite:148). The lever `l-hiring-ahead-exposure-cap` plans payroll against the 30-day default and not the 15-day goal [202](#cite:202) [201](#cite:201).

short: The FAR 32.009 policy that agencies pay small business contractors with a goal of 15 days after a proper invoice, and that primes pass it to small subcontractors.
definition: Agencies shall provide accelerated payments to small business contractors, to the fullest extent permitted by law, with a goal of 15 days after receipt of a proper invoice, and to prime contractors that agree to pay their small business subcontractors within 15 days of receiving the accelerated payment; the acceleration creates no new Prompt Payment Act rights [201](#cite:201). The plan-stage gate `prompt-payment-and-accelerated-payment` reads the 15-day figure as a goal against the 30-day default, and the lever on hiring-ahead exposure asks for it where it applies [201](#cite:201) [202](#cite:202).

short: A contract or order reserved for small business under a program status; on a services set-aside the prime keeps at least half the amount paid.
definition: A small business set-aside or sole-source services contract carries the limitations-on-subcontracting clause: the prime will not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the government for contract performance to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities, measured by the end of the base term and each option period, or of each order [198](#cite:198). The clause applies to set-aside and sole-source contracts and orders under FAR subparts 19.5, 19.8, 19.13, 19.14 and 19.15 [198](#cite:198). The plan-stage record `c-partner-support-limits` reads the limit as the first of three bounds on partner support, with consent and the no-poach rule the others [198](#cite:198) [199](#cite:199) [187](#cite:187).

short: The firm holding the government contract and answering for its performance, with subcontractors and teammates working under it.
definition: The prime holds the contract with the government: on a set-aside it answers for the subcontracting limit [198](#cite:198), it needs the contracting officer's advance consent before a cost-type, time-and-materials or labor-hour subcontract where it has no approved purchasing system, and consent does not relieve it of responsibility for performance [199](#cite:199). A prime that receives accelerated payment passes it to small business subcontractors within 15 days [201](#cite:201). On a T&M contract not competitively awarded, the prime, each subcontractor and each affiliate bill at separate labor-category rates [98](#cite:98). In the retain records the prime or a teammate may hire the firm's trained people, and an agreement with either not to do so is illegal [187](#cite:187).

short: A firm that contracts with a prime to furnish supplies or services for performance of the prime contract.
definition: A subcontract is any contract entered into by a subcontractor to furnish supplies or services for performance of the prime contract, and a cost-type, time-and-materials or labor-hour subcontract needs the contracting officer's advance consent where the prime has no approved purchasing system [199](#cite:199). On a set-aside, payments to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities are capped at 50 percent of the amount paid for services; a similarly situated entity shares the prime's program status and is small under the subcontract's NAICS code [198](#cite:198). A subcontractor's labor bills at its own category rates on a T&M contract not competitively awarded [98](#cite:98), and a small subcontractor is owed accelerated payment within 15 days of the prime receiving it [201](#cite:201). A clearance may not be requested for a subcontractor's employees [119](#cite:119).

short: The re-competition of a contract at the end of its term; a visible end date that the retain records treat as a withdrawal cognition.
definition: The pack uses the term for the point at which a contract is competed again: rate relief can come through the adjustment clause, a modification, or repricing at option or recompete, a step the offer records mark as synthesis [117](#cite:117) [98](#cite:98). An employee on a contract with a known end date, a recompete or a protest carries the two strongest predictors of leaving, wanting to leave (ρ .56) and the alternatives a person sees (.23) [178](#cite:178). A worker on a lost recompete has no federal claim on the successor's payroll since the nondisplacement order's revocation, and the retain lever `l-honest-pipeline-communication` communicates option years, recompetes and protests as facts with dates [186](#cite:186).

short: The contractor that takes over a service contract after a recompete; it owes the Service Contract Act floors but no right of first refusal to the incumbent's staff.
definition: Executive Order 14055 had given qualified employees on a federal service contract a right of first refusal with the successor contractor; EO 14148 revoked it on January 20, 2025, the Department of Labor removed 29 CFR part 9 effective December 22, 2025, and the FAR Council had never issued the implementing clause, so the right never bound contractors [186](#cite:186). The Service Contract Act's wage and benefit floors still attach to the successor contract [101](#cite:101). The handover gate `service-contract-transition-rules` carries one step: no implied right of first refusal, and the successor's terms stated as unknown until known [186](#cite:186).

short: The former federal rule giving service-contract employees a right of first refusal with a successor contractor; revoked in 2025 and rescinded December 22, 2025.
definition: Nondisplacement of qualified workers was the policy of Executive Order 14055, under which qualified employees on a federal service contract had a right of first refusal of employment with the successor contractor; EO 14148 of January 20, 2025 revoked it, the FAR Council never issued implementing regulations, and the Department of Labor removed and reserved 29 CFR part 9 effective December 22, 2025 without notice and comment, estimating year-one net savings of \$39.12 million [186](#cite:186). The changes file records the rescission as `ch-025` and corrects an earlier note that had attributed the revocation to EO 14236 [186](#cite:186). The retain-stage record `c-contract-discontinuity-fear` reads the loss of the right as part of what a visible contract end now means to an employee [186](#cite:186) [178](#cite:178).

short: The federal electronic work-authorization check; FAR clause 52.222-54 requires it on contracts over $150,000 lasting 120 days or more with work in the United States.
definition: The E-Verify clause goes into solicitations and contracts exceeding \$150,000 except work performed only outside the United States, periods of performance under 120 days, and commercial and COTS items [129](#cite:129). A contractor not yet enrolled enrolls as a federal contractor within 30 calendar days of award; new hires are verified within 3 business days after the date of hire; employees assigned to the contract are verified within 90 calendar days of enrollment or award or 30 days after assignment, whichever is later; no re-verification is required for an employee already verified, holding an active Confidential, Secret or Top Secret clearance, or credentialed after a completed HSPD-12 investigation; and the clause flows down to service and construction subcontracts over \$3,500 performed in the United States [128](#cite:128). The clear-start lever `l-start-date-compliance-sequence` places the check within three business days of hire, alongside the Form I-9 steps [128](#cite:128) [130](#cite:130).

short: The employment eligibility verification form every U.S. hire completes; Section 2 is due within three business days of the start, with the employee choosing the documents.
definition: Section 2 of Form I-9 must be completed within three business days of the date employment begins, and on the first day for a job of fewer than three business days; the employee chooses which acceptable documents to present and the employer cannot specify them; the documents are examined in the employee's physical presence unless the employer qualifies for the alternative procedure open to E-Verify participants; and receipts are accepted for a limited period [130](#cite:130). The Justice Department's export-control fact sheet keeps any export assessment separate from the Form I-9 process and warns against limiting document choice [131](#cite:131). The gate record notes that the Section 1 page failed to fetch, so its first-day rule is carried from the Section 2 page's structure [130](#cite:130).

short: Under ITAR, releasing or transferring technical data to a foreign person in the United States is an export to every country of that person's citizenship or permanent residency.
definition: Under 22 CFR 120.50, releasing or otherwise transferring technical data to a foreign person in the United States is an export, deemed to go to every country of the person's citizenship or permanent residency [132](#cite:132). The hiring consequence is that a non-U.S. person cannot start on controlled work until the employer has applied to State or Commerce for an authorization, and the assessment of who is a U.S. person is made only for positions that work with controlled items, apart from the Form I-9 [131](#cite:131). The clear-start constraint `c-foreign-national-hire-blocked` carries the license, the clearance and the visa as three clocks the firm does not run [132](#cite:132) [119](#cite:119) [142](#cite:142).

short: The International Traffic in Arms Regulations at 22 CFR, whose deemed-export rule and U.S.-person definition shape hiring for controlled work.
definition: The International Traffic in Arms Regulations define an export to include releasing technical data to a foreign person in the United States [132](#cite:132), and define a U.S. person as a lawful permanent resident or a protected individual under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3), which reaches citizens, nationals, refugees and asylees [133](#cite:133). The regulations contain no hiring requirements, so a posting that limits ITAR work to U.S. citizens, or to citizens and permanent residents, violates the citizenship-status rule unless a law or government contract requires the restriction [131](#cite:131) [49](#cite:49). Settlements for such postings ran from \$365,000 to \$500,000 per employer in 2023, with more than \$2.5 million across job-platform users [49](#cite:49).

short: The second export-control regime the hiring rules name beside ITAR, cited at 15 CFR parts 734 and 772; it contains no hiring requirement.
definition: The pack carries the EAR through the hiring rules that apply to both export regimes: the Justice Department's fact sheet states that ITAR and EAR contain no hiring requirements, that a posting must not say the export rules require a citizenship, that only positions working with controlled items are assessed, and that an authorization is sought from State or Commerce before a non-U.S. person does the work [131](#cite:131). The gates cite the EAR at 15 CFR 772 for its U.S.-person definition and at 15 CFR part 734 [131](#cite:131) [133](#cite:133). An ITAR or EAR posting limited to citizens and permanent residents was the subject of a 2023 Justice Department settlement [50](#cite:50).

short: For export control, a lawful permanent resident or a protected individual under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3): citizens, nationals, permanent residents, refugees and asylees.
definition: Under 22 CFR 120.62 a U.S. person is a lawful permanent resident or a protected individual under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3), plus entities incorporated to do business in the United States and government entities [133](#cite:133). The Justice Department's fact sheet lists U.S. persons for export purposes as citizens, nationals, lawful permanent residents, refugees and asylees, and tells employers not to state that export rules require a citizenship [131](#cite:131). Because the export definition matches the protected-individual definition in the anti-discrimination statute, a "citizens only" posting for ITAR or EAR work has no good-faith exception [49](#cite:49). The Title VII national security exception covers a clearance condition but not a citizenship restriction the law does not require [140](#cite:140) [131](#cite:131).

short: The work visa for foreign professionals; a $100,000 entry payment was extended on September 21, 2026 but is uncollected under a court vacatur, and a $103,265 fee is proposed.
definition: The September 2025 proclamation restricted entry of certain H-1B workers outside the United States unless the petition carried a \$100,000 payment, and a new proclamation effective September 21, 2026 extends the restriction twelve months [142](#cite:142). The District of Massachusetts vacated the implementing policy in its entirety on June 8, 2026 and the First Circuit denied a stay on July 24, 2026, so the payment is not being collected while the appeal proceeds [143](#cite:143); the D.C. district court upheld the proclamation on December 23, 2025 and that appeal is pending [226](#cite:226). USCIS separately proposed a \$103,265 fee on cap-subject petitions on August 25, 2026, not final as of the sweep [141](#cite:141). The clear-start record `c-foreign-national-hire-blocked` carries the visa as one of three clocks outside the firm's control [142](#cite:142) [143](#cite:143) [141](#cite:141).

variants: Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs
short: The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs, the DOL office whose 2026 rules rescinded the EO 11246 regulations and updated Section 503 and VEVRAA.
definition: The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs is the Department of Labor office behind the contractor compliance framework; its final rule of August 21, 2026 removes the regulations issued under Executive Order 11246 effective October 26, 2026 [86](#cite:86), and its two companion rules narrow Section 503 and update VEVRAA effective September 21, 2026 [55](#cite:55). With part 60-1 go the Internet Applicant definition and the online-recruiting record-keeping rule of 2006 [86](#cite:86) [87](#cite:87). The changes file records the three rules as `ch-004` [86](#cite:86) [55](#cite:55).

short: The contractor affirmative-action order revoked by EO 14173 in January 2025; its implementing regulations are removed effective October 26, 2026.
definition: Executive Order 11246 was the affirmative-action executive order for federal contractors; EO 14173 revoked it in January 2025 [86](#cite:86) [55](#cite:55). The OFCCP final rule of August 21, 2026 removes 41 CFR parts 60-1, 60-2, 60-3, 60-4, 60-20, 60-40, 60-50 and 60-999 and strips the order's content from part 60-30, effective October 26, 2026, on the ground that the revocation alone is sufficient [86](#cite:86). Part 60-1 held the Internet Applicant definition and the online-recruiting record-keeping rule effective February 6, 2006, so those go with it; what remains for contractors is statutory, Section 503 and VEVRAA, with Title VII and the Uniform Guidelines unchanged [86](#cite:86) [87](#cite:87) [55](#cite:55).

variants: Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act
Vietnam Era Veterans Readjustment Assistance Act
short: The Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act, whose clause requires a covered contractor to list every opening with the state workforce agency; threshold $200,000 from 2026.
definition: A contractor covered by the Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act lists every employment opening, at every establishment and whether or not it is contract-funded, with the appropriate employment service delivery system at least concurrently with any other recruiting; listing with the state workforce agency job bank satisfies the duty, and executive and senior management positions, positions filled from within and positions of three days or less are excepted [73](#cite:73). The contractor tells the delivery system that it is a federal contractor and wants priority referral of protected veterans [73](#cite:73). The 2026 final rule, effective September 21, 2026, sets the coverage threshold at \$200,000 and keeps the written affirmative action plan and the veteran applicant and hire reporting, while the printed clause still shows a \$100,000 subcontract flow-down figure [55](#cite:55) [73](#cite:73).

short: The statutory contractor requirement that survives the EO 11246 rescission with a written plan at 50 employees and a $50,000 contract; its 7 percent goal is rescinded.
definition: Section 503 is one of the two statutory contractor requirements left after the EO 11246 regulations are removed: the 2026 final rule, effective September 21, 2026, narrows it by rescinding the 7 percent utilization goal and the applicant self-identification solicitation, sets the coverage threshold at \$20,000, and keeps the written affirmative action plan at 50 employees and a \$50,000 contract [55](#cite:55). The gate `eeo-contractor-framework-2026` carries those terms from a law-firm alert pending the Federal Register notices [55](#cite:55) [86](#cite:86). The pack does not describe the statute's subject beyond these thresholds.

short: Title VII §703(g): refusing to hire or discharging someone for a position subject to a national-security requirement they do not meet is not unlawful.
definition: Under 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2(g), it is not an unlawful employment practice to refuse to hire or to discharge an individual for a position subject to a requirement imposed in the interest of national security under a statute or executive order where the individual has not fulfilled or has ceased to fulfill that requirement [140](#cite:140). The exception covers the clearance condition on an offer; it does not cover a citizenship restriction the law does not require, which remains a citizenship-status violation [140](#cite:140) [131](#cite:131) [49](#cite:49). The EEOC's criminal-records guidance reads it as reaching only positions actually subject to federal security requirements, where the action followed a clearance denial [47](#cite:47).

short: The federal law governing employer use of third-party background reports: stand-alone disclosure, written permission and the two-notice adverse-action sequence.
definition: Before obtaining a consumer report, an employer gives a written, stand-alone disclosure that is not part of the application, obtains written permission, and certifies compliance to the reporting company; before taking an adverse action it gives the person a copy of the report and the summary of rights so the person can dispute it; after the action it sends a notice with the reporting company's name and contact, a statement that the company did not make the decision, and the rights to dispute and to a free report within 60 days [136](#cite:136). Investigative reports built on interviews carry extra notices, and some states restrict credit reports in hiring [136](#cite:136). The FTC states no waiting period between the two notices; the gate flags that state law and case law supply one in practice [136](#cite:136).

short: A third-party background report on an applicant, governed by the FCRA's disclosure, permission and notice rules.
definition: A consumer report is the background report an employer obtains from a reporting company, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act attaches duties to each step: a written, stand-alone disclosure and written permission before the report is ordered, a certification to the reporting company, and the pre-adverse-action and adverse-action notices before and after any decision against the person [136](#cite:136). Investigative reports built on interviews carry extra notices [136](#cite:136). The clear-start constraint `c-start-date-compliance-clocks` lists a background check ordered on the application form's consent language as a sign the sequence has gone wrong [136](#cite:136).

short: The FCRA notice sent after a decision against the person based on a consumer report, preceded by a pre-adverse-action notice with the report and the rights summary.
definition: Before taking an adverse action based on a consumer report, the employer gives the person a copy of the report and the FCRA summary of rights so the person can dispute it; after the action it sends a notice with the reporting company's name and contact, a statement that the company did not make the decision, and the person's rights to dispute the report and to a free report within 60 days [136](#cite:136). The FTC guidance states no waiting period between the two notices, and the gate records that state law and case law supply one in practice [136](#cite:136). A step taken out of order is itself a violation, which the constraint `c-start-date-compliance-clocks` marks as synthesis from the guidance [136](#cite:136).

short: A state or local law requiring a pay range in the job posting itself; fourteen states and DC by October 2026, with Delaware in 2027.
definition: A pay-range posting law requires the range in the posting itself; the 2026 law-firm map lists California (15 or more employees), Colorado, Delaware (26 or more, from September 26, 2027), Hawaii (50 or more), Illinois (15 or more), Maryland, Massachusetts (25 or more), Minnesota (30 or more), New Jersey (10 or more), New York (4 or more), Vermont (5 or more), Washington (15 or more) and the District of Columbia, with local rules in Ohio cities and parts of New Jersey and New York [76](#cite:76). Three states joined in 2026: Virginia from July 1 for all employers, with a salary-history ban and a private right of action after a 15-day cure notice; Maine from July 29 for employers of ten or more; and Connecticut from October 1 under PA 26-12 for all employers, with a benefits description [223](#cite:223) [224](#cite:224). Posting laws raised disclosure by about 30 percentage points and wages by 1.3 to 3.6 percent with no effect on employment or postings in the one difference-in-differences study [97](#cite:97). Every state row rests on compilations with the statutes pending [76](#cite:76) [207](#cite:207).

short: A state or local law barring employers from asking applicants about prior pay; about twenty statewide bans, with Virginia added July 1, 2026.
definition: About twenty states bar all employers from asking applicants about salary history, with public-employer-only bans elsewhere and local ordinances on top; several states permit asking or confirming only after an offer, and Michigan and Wisconsin have ended bans for most employers [106](#cite:106). The early bans raised women's earnings relative to men's by about 1 percent, mainly among job changers, in a difference-in-differences study of the first adopting states [96](#cite:96). Virginia's 2026 pay-transparency law bars salary-history inquiries and reliance for all employers from July 1, 2026 [223](#cite:223). In the Ninth Circuit prior pay is not a factor other than sex under the Equal Pay Act, and the pack's reading, marked as synthesis, is that an offer anchored on prior pay is both barred to ask about in many states and indefensible as a justification in that circuit [116](#cite:116) [106](#cite:106). The jurisdiction list rests on a vendor page and the Mercer roundup, which disagree on Missouri [106](#cite:106) [207](#cite:207).

short: The federal law requiring equal pay for substantially equal work in the same establishment, with four defenses and no cure by cutting anyone's pay.
definition: Men and women must receive equal pay for substantially equal work, judged by skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions, in the same establishment; differences are lawful only on seniority, merit, quantity or quality of production, or a factor other than sex; the employer carries the burden; and no one's pay may be reduced to close a gap [112](#cite:112). Job content, not job titles, decides whether jobs are substantially equal [112](#cite:112). In the Ninth Circuit prior salary, alone or in combination, is not a factor other than sex, while the Seventh Circuit holds otherwise [116](#cite:116). Title VII, the ADEA and the ADA also prohibit pay discrimination, without the same-establishment or substantially-equal requirements [112](#cite:112).

short: The narrowing of pay differences between new hires and incumbents, or across peers, that a market-rate offer creates and the law forbids curing downward.
definition: Pay compression is what a market-rate offer does to the people already in the job: external hires started about 18 percent higher than workers promoted into similar jobs at the one firm measured, performed worse for two years and left more often [93](#cite:93), and employees who learn they earn less than their unit's median lose satisfaction and search for other jobs while those above gain nothing [92](#cite:92). Under state right-to-discuss laws wages run about 2 percent lower as employers hold the line to avoid renegotiating with everyone [90](#cite:90). The Equal Pay Act closes the downward cure, since no one's pay may be reduced to close a gap [112](#cite:112). The offer stage carries a compression-ratio metric, new-hire pay over incumbent pay in substantially equal jobs [93](#cite:93).

short: The FAR subpart 26.5 duty on larger contracts: a policy, an awareness program and conviction reporting, with no testing; the DFARS testing clause was reserved in May 2026.
definition: Contracts above the simplified acquisition threshold, other than commercial products and services and work outside the United States, require a policy statement, an awareness program, employee reporting of workplace drug convictions within 5 days, notice to the contracting officer within 10 days and action within 30 days, with compliance within 30 days of award; the subpart requires no drug testing [135](#cite:135). The DFARS clause that required DoD contractors on classified and other sensitive work to run a testing program, 252.223-7004, is reserved as of the May 7, 2026 DFARS change, and Part 223 no longer carries the drug-free work force subpart; the rulemaking that removed it was not found [134](#cite:134). The gate concludes, as synthesis, that testing is a matter of firm policy and state law unless a customer writes a requirement into the contract [135](#cite:135) [134](#cite:134).

short: A state law protecting off-duty cannabis use or barring pre-employment THC tests; nine adult-use states have one, and every one excepts federal contracts and clearance work.
definition: Nine adult-use states protect off-duty cannabis use or restrict pre-employment THC tests, with statute citations in the compilation the overlay rests on: California, Connecticut, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Washington; each excepts federal contracts, funding or clearance work and safety-sensitive roles, and medical anti-discrimination provisions are listed for twenty-two states [219](#cite:219). Washington's statute, for example, bars rejecting applicants for off-hours use or non-psychoactive metabolite results but excepts jobs requiring a federal background investigation or clearance [219](#cite:219). Every row is flagged primary-pending because the source is an advocacy compilation [219](#cite:219). Federally, the drug-free workplace subpart requires no testing and the DFARS testing clause is reserved [135](#cite:135) [134](#cite:134).

short: A state law limiting employer credit checks; the vendor map lists thirteen states, DC and Puerto Rico, several excepting positions that require a security clearance.
definition: Statewide limits on employer credit checks are listed for Washington, Hawaii, Oregon, Illinois, Connecticut, Maryland, California, Vermont, Colorado, Nevada, Delaware, Massachusetts and New York State, plus the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, with Rhode Island requiring disclosure only and local ordinances in Chicago, Cook County, Madison, New York City and Philadelphia; typical exceptions cover financial institutions, managerial roles, fiduciary roles and positions requiring a security clearance [218](#cite:218). New York's statewide law took effect April 18, 2026, joining the city's 2015 ordinance, and Massachusetts's limit took effect January 1, 2025 [218](#cite:218). The federal FCRA notice sequence applies in every state, and the vendor map carries no statute citations, so every row is flagged primary-pending [218](#cite:218) [136](#cite:136).

short: The duty to keep application and selection records: one year from the record or the action under 29 CFR 1602.14, longer once a charge is filed, four years under California's ADS rules.
definition: Application forms and records of hiring, promotion, demotion, transfer, lay-off, termination, pay and selection for training or apprenticeship are kept one year from the making of the record or the personnel action, whichever is later; an involuntarily terminated employee's records one year from termination; and all relevant records until final disposition once a charge is filed or an action brought [200](#cite:200). The Uniform Guidelines require records by race, sex and ethnic group sufficient to compute adverse impact [31](#cite:31), and California's automated-decision rules extend retention of ADS records from two to four years [40](#cite:40). The contractor-specific record duties under the EO 11246 regulations, the Internet Applicant rule among them, go with those regulations on October 26, 2026 [86](#cite:86). The plan-stage record `c-decisions-on-anecdote` notes that the law already requires most of the record a firm would need to replace anecdote [200](#cite:200) [31](#cite:31).

short: Eligibility for access to classified information, requested by a sponsoring contractor for an employee a classified contract needs and decided by the government.
definition: Under the NISPOM rule a contractor may request eligibility for access to classified information only where the access is essential to a classified contract, for the minimum number of employees, and never to build a cache of cleared staff [119](#cite:119). No individual can initiate a clearance; only a sponsoring agency or contractor can [80](#cite:80). The last public count put about 4.2 million holders in October 2019, 1,346,765 of them contractors or other, with 672,656 at top secret [80](#cite:80). An eligibility granted elsewhere moves by reciprocity under SEAD 7 [122](#cite:122), and a cleared employee's termination and any adverse information must be reported under 32 CFR 117.8 [189](#cite:189).

short: The distinction the pack draws between a favorable eligibility determination and the separate decisions, by separate owners, that put the hire at a desk.
definition:
<!-- synthesis -->
A favorable eligibility determination lets the firm grant access to classified information, but the constraint `c-eligibility-is-not-access` carries the separate decisions that still stand between the hire and the work. A Common Access Card needs a government sponsor and is issued only after a favorable fingerprint check with an investigation already submitted [138](#cite:138), an interim card does not transfer between sponsors [137](#cite:137), a clearance held elsewhere needs a reciprocity decision the rule puts at five business days [122](#cite:122) that agencies do not reliably track [145](#cite:145), SCI and SAP access on a temporary basis is a separate decision of the granting authority [119](#cite:119), and a cyber work role needs its foundational qualification on the day the work starts [139](#cite:139). At DHS the interval from a favorable determination to onboarding ran 41 days in FY2026 Q3 [125](#cite:125).

short: The entity eligibility determination a firm must hold before it can sponsor anyone; the firm cannot apply for it, a contracting activity or a cleared prime sponsors it.
definition: A contractor cannot apply for its own entity eligibility determination; a government contracting activity or a cleared contractor sponsors it when the firm needs access to compete or perform, on a legitimate government requirement [120](#cite:120) [146](#cite:146). The firm must be organized under U.S. law with a record of integrity, its senior management official, facility security officer and insider-threat official must hold eligibility, and foreign ownership, control or influence must not be disqualifying [120](#cite:120). DCSA's roadmap puts the package review in NISS at day 20 and the key officials' questionnaires and fingerprints at day 45, with the government funding the processing and no end-to-end time stated [146](#cite:146). While a determination is invalidated the firm may not bid on new classified work [120](#cite:120).

short: The request a cleared contractor makes for an employee's eligibility, allowed only for access a classified contract needs; a candidate cannot start a clearance alone.
definition: Sponsorship is the request through which a person is cleared: an individual may not obtain or initiate a security clearance on their own [80](#cite:80), and a contractor may request eligibility only where access is essential to a classified contract, for the minimum number of employees, never for non-employees or subcontractor employees, and never to build a cache of cleared staff [119](#cite:119). A request before employment needs a written commitment the candidate accepted in writing, and employment must begin within 45 days of the grant [119](#cite:119). The request itself requires a facility clearance that a contracting activity or a cleared prime has sponsored on a bona fide need, with the DD 254 or pre-award authorization behind it [146](#cite:146). The lever `l-confirm-sponsorship-path-before-posting` carries the three paths a hire can take: reciprocity of a current eligibility, temporary eligibility pending investigation, or a full investigation [119](#cite:119) [122](#cite:122).

short: The National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual, now the rule at 32 CFR part 117, which fixes who a contractor can get cleared, when, and what it must report.
definition: The National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual rule at 32 CFR part 117 is the regulation the clear-start and handover stages run on. Section 117.10 fixes who a contractor can get cleared and when: a request only for access essential to a classified contract, a pre-employment investigation only on a written commitment with a start within 45 days of the grant, temporary eligibility only where nothing adverse has surfaced, and a non-U.S. citizen only by Limited Access Authorization in rare cases [119](#cite:119). Section 117.9 says a firm cannot apply for its own facility clearance and must be sponsored [120](#cite:120), and section 117.8 lists what the contractor reports, including terminations and adverse information that must be reported even after the employee has left [189](#cite:189).

short: The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, whose industry investigations, vetting systems and timeliness figures set the clock a sponsored hire waits on.
definition: The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency is the agency whose industry cases the clearance clock measures: its initial cases averaged 197 days end to end for a Secret and 243 for a Top Secret in FY2026 Q3, on the all-cases basis adopted that quarter, with adjudication the longest phase [126](#cite:126) [125](#cite:125). Its Facility Clearance Branch publishes the roadmap by which a sponsored firm gets a facility clearance [146](#cite:146), and its systems page indexes the vetting and industrial-security systems a facility security officer uses [149](#cite:149). Its investigation inventory stood at about 121,000 in FY2026 Q3 [54](#cite:54), and GAO found that its timeliness method understated processing time from 2020 to 2024 [56](#cite:56).

short: The government's end-to-end personnel vetting system, with eApp as its electronic questionnaire; its roadmap runs to Trusted Workforce 2.0 full operating capability in FY2028 Q1.
definition: NBIS is the end-to-end personnel vetting system DCSA describes on its systems page, alongside the system that shows investigations and determinations and the fingerprint transmission to the FBI [149](#cite:149). The NISPPAC roadmap slide names DISS-JVS, eApp and the Individual Engagement Platform within it, with eInterview due in FY2027 Q2, expanded eVetting in FY2027 Q3 and Trusted Workforce 2.0 full operating capability in FY2028 Q1 [125](#cite:125); the quarterly report puts eVetting for preliminary determinations in August 2026 and the Individual Engagement Platform in September 2026 [54](#cite:54). The government funds the processing of personnel and facility clearances [146](#cite:146).

short: The system in which a facility security officer sees investigations and personnel security determinations; DISS in the 2022 roadmap, DISS-JVS on the NBIS roadmap.
definition: DISS is the system DCSA describes as the one that shows investigations and personnel security determinations, one of the systems a facility security officer uses to sponsor and track a hire [149](#cite:149). The 2022 facility-clearance roadmap names it together with e-QIP [146](#cite:146), and the September 2026 NISPPAC roadmap slide names DISS-JVS alongside eApp within NBIS [125](#cite:125). The enabler `dcsa-personnel-vetting-systems` lists it with the sponsorship, two-track, temporary-eligibility, reciprocity and pre-start levers it serves [149](#cite:149) [146](#cite:146).

short: The electronic questionnaire within NBIS through which a sponsored hire submits the investigative form; the 2022 roadmap calls the questionnaire system e-QIP.
definition: eApp is the electronic questionnaire named on the NISPPAC's NBIS roadmap slide, beside DISS-JVS and the Individual Engagement Platform [125](#cite:125); DCSA's systems page describes the vetting system's questionnaire and the submission of investigative standard forms without naming them [149](#cite:149). The 2022 facility-clearance roadmap names the questionnaire system e-QIP and sets day 45 as the deadline for the key officials' e-QIP and fingerprint submission [146](#cite:146). The temporary-eligibility lever asks for the questionnaire and fingerprints to be submitted as early as the written commitment allows, since the interim determination follows the initial checks [119](#cite:119) [146](#cite:146).

short: The questionnaire a sponsored hire submits, with fingerprints, to start the investigation; the pack's sources call it the questionnaire or the investigative standard form.
definition: The pack's sources do not name the form by its number; they describe the questionnaire a sponsored hire submits with fingerprints to start the investigation, the investigative standard forms submitted through the vetting system [149](#cite:149), and the e-QIP and fingerprint submission the facility-clearance roadmap requires from the key officials by day 45 [146](#cite:146). The determination of temporary eligibility follows the initial checks on that submission, and is granted only where no adverse information is found [119](#cite:119) [146](#cite:146). The Individual Engagement Platform is to carry a five-year questionnaire update from September 2026 under the Trusted Workforce 2.0 milestones [54](#cite:54).

short: Interim eligibility granted before the final determination, only where no adverse information appears, for up to a year, not valid for RD, COMSEC or NATO information, and withdrawable without appeal.
definition: Government-wide policy on temporary eligibility dates from Security Executive Agent Directive 8 of May 18, 2020 [121](#cite:121); for contractors it is implemented at 32 CFR 117.10(l), under which it is granted only where no adverse information is found, limited to one year without approval, valid at its level but not for RD, COMSEC or NATO information until the final grant, with SCI and SAP access a separate decision of the granting authority, non-U.S. citizens ineligible, and withdrawal neither a denial nor appealable [119](#cite:119). No public figure reports how often a contractor applicant receives one or how long the decision takes [127](#cite:127). An interim held elsewhere is an exception to reciprocity [122](#cite:122), and an interim credential does not transfer between sponsors [137](#cite:137).

short: The SEAD 7 rule that an agency accepts another authorized agency's investigation and adjudication, decided within five business days, unless one of seven exceptions applies.
definition: Under SEAD 7 an agency accepts a background investigation and a national security adjudication by an authorized agency unless an exception applies: new adjudicatively relevant information, an investigation more than seven years old, an adjudication recorded with an exception, a Bond Amendment disqualifier where SCI, SAP or RD access is needed, an agency-specific requirement the Security Executive Agent approved, an interim, limited or one-time grant, or a current denial or revocation [122](#cite:122). The determination is due within five business days of receipt, polygraphs are reciprocally accepted, and reciprocity cannot be denied for want of one [122](#cite:122). GAO found the government's reciprocity data inconsistent and incomplete, with 28 of 31 surveyed agencies saying their systems at times lacked the needed information and contractors left without status updates [145](#cite:145). The two-track lever sets reciprocity's five business days against the 197-to-243-day investigation clock [122](#cite:122) [126](#cite:126).

short: Enrollment of cleared people in standing checks under Trusted Workforce 2.0: 78 percent of the covered population in FY2026 Q3, with full enrollment planned for September 2028.
definition: Continuous vetting is the enrollment the Trusted Workforce 2.0 program tracks: 78 percent of the covered population and 54 percent of the national-security population were enrolled in FY2026 Q3, with industry at about 984,000 enrollments, roughly a quarter of the TW 1.5 population, and full enrollment planned for September 2028 [54](#cite:54) [126](#cite:126). The quarterly report attributes part of the rise in the investigation inventory to follow-up on continuous-vetting alerts [54](#cite:54). The gate `nispom-reporting-and-continuous-vetting` pairs it with the SEAD 3 self-reporting duties of the cleared employee and the contractor's reporting duties under 32 CFR 117.8 [190](#cite:190) [189](#cite:189).

short: The government-wide personnel-vetting reform whose quarterly report sets the 40- and 75-day timeliness targets and whose milestones run to full operating capability in FY2028 Q1.
definition: Trusted Workforce 2.0 is the reform the Performance Accountability Council reports on quarterly: end-to-end targets of 40 days for a moderate-risk and 75 for a high-risk position, a timeliness series that switched in FY2026 Q3 from the fastest 90 percent of cases to all cases, and a milestone table running through eVetting in August 2026, the Individual Engagement Platform in September 2026 and full continuous-vetting enrollment in September 2028 [54](#cite:54). The NBIS roadmap places full operating capability in FY2028 Q1 [125](#cite:125). The report's own words are that performance "remains much too high compared to performance targets" [54](#cite:54), and the controversy record `clearance-timeliness-figures` sets its government-wide figures against DCSA's industry figures [54](#cite:54) [126](#cite:126).

short: The thirteen SEAD 4 guidelines, weighed under the whole-person concept, against which every eligibility decision is made; financial issues are the most common in appeals.
definition: Thirteen guidelines under SEAD 4 govern every eligibility decision: allegiance, foreign influence, foreign preference, sexual behavior, personal conduct, financial considerations, alcohol, drug involvement, psychological conditions, criminal conduct, handling protected information, outside activities and use of information technology, each with listed conditions that raise and that mitigate a concern, weighed under the whole-person concept [123](#cite:123). The guidelines apply to contractors as covered individuals [123](#cite:123). A vendor's count of 624 published DOHA appeal decisions for 2024 found financial issues outnumbered all other issues combined [151](#cite:151). Adjudication was the longest phase of an industry case in FY2026 Q3, 117 days for a Secret and 126 for a Top Secret [126](#cite:126).

short: The statute that bars eligibility outright for an unlawful drug user or addict, with no waiver, and bars SCI, SAP and RD access after a year's incarceration or a dishonorable discharge.
definition: The Bond Amendment, 50 U.S.C. 3343, bars eligibility outright for an unlawful drug user or addict, with no waiver, and bars SCI, SAP and RD access for a person sentenced to a year or more of incarceration, dishonorably discharged, or found mentally incompetent, as SEAD 4's Appendix B sets out [123](#cite:123). A Bond Amendment disqualifier is one of the exceptions to reciprocity where SCI, SAP or RD access is needed [122](#cite:122).

short: A lie-detector examination the government may administer to defense and intelligence contractor staff; scheduled after a preliminary determination and never a ground for denying reciprocity.
definition: The Employee Polygraph Protection Act's national-security exemption lets the federal government administer a lie detector test, in a counterintelligence function, to any employee of a DoD contractor, and, in an intelligence or counterintelligence function, to employees of contractors of NSA, DIA, NGA or CIA and to contractor staff whose duties involve Top Secret or special-access information [147](#cite:147). Under SEAD 7 polygraphs are accepted when they match the receiving agency's requirement, reciprocity cannot be denied for want of one, and the polygraph is scheduled after a preliminary determination [122](#cite:122). In the 2025 cleared-compensation survey a full-scope polygraph went with average pay of \$141,299 [89](#cite:89).

short: Information to which access is a separate read-in beyond the clearance level: SCI access on a temporary basis is the granting authority's own decision, and a Bond Amendment disqualifier bars it.
definition: SCI access is a decision apart from the clearance level: under 32 CFR 117.10(l) SCI and SAP access on a temporary basis is a separate decision of the granting authority [119](#cite:119), a Bond Amendment disqualifier bars SCI, SAP and RD access [123](#cite:123), and such a disqualifier is an exception to reciprocity where SCI, SAP or RD access is needed [122](#cite:122). The constraint `c-eligibility-is-not-access` lists a needed SCI or SAP read-in the candidate does not hold among the things that keep an eligible hire from the work [119](#cite:119). In the 2025 cleared-compensation survey, TS/SCI holders averaged \$132,177 against \$124,084 for Top Secret, about \$31,900 over Secret [89](#cite:89).

short: The higher clearance level: an industry Top Secret took 243 days end to end in FY2026 Q3, paid an average $124,084 in the 2025 survey, and is never available to a non-U.S. citizen.
definition: An industry Top Secret case averaged 243 days from initiation to adjudication in FY2026 Q3, 20 days of initiation, 97 of investigation and 126 of adjudication, against 227 days on the earlier fastest-90-percent basis in FY2026 Q1 [126](#cite:126) [124](#cite:124). A non-U.S. citizen can hold only a Limited Access Authorization and never Top Secret [119](#cite:119). Cleared professionals with a Top Secret averaged \$124,084 in the 2025 compensation survey, about \$23,800 over Secret [89](#cite:89); of the 1,346,765 contractor and other clearance holders counted in October 2019, 672,656 held top secret [80](#cite:80). The polygraph exemption reaches contractor staff whose duties involve Top Secret or special-access information [147](#cite:147).

short: The clearance level whose industry cases took 197 days end to end in FY2026 Q3; average pay $100,296 in the 2025 survey, about $9,500 over Confidential.
definition: An industry Secret case averaged 197 days from initiation to adjudication in FY2026 Q3, 21 days of initiation, 59 of investigation and 117 of adjudication, against 156 days on the fastest-90-percent basis in FY2026 Q1 [126](#cite:126) [124](#cite:124). A temporary Secret is valid at that level but not for RD, COMSEC or NATO information until the final grant [119](#cite:119). Holders averaged \$100,296 in the 2025 compensation survey, about \$9,500 over Confidential and \$23,800 below Top Secret [89](#cite:89), and the 2019 count put 2,859,877 people at confidential or secret [80](#cite:80). An employee holding an active Confidential, Secret or Top Secret clearance needs no E-Verify re-verification [128](#cite:128).

short: DCSA's count of pending background investigations: about 121,000 in FY2026 Q3, up from about 101,000 the prior quarter.
definition: The investigation inventory is DCSA's count of pending background investigations, about 121,000 in FY2026 Q3, up from about 101,000 the quarter before, which the quarterly report attributes to demand for initial investigations and follow-up on continuous-vetting alerts and says risks slowing timeliness further [54](#cite:54) [126](#cite:126). The eight-quarter series from FY2025 Q4 reads 259, 244, 215, 203, 162, 109, 101 and 121 thousand, with the labels inferred from the chart order [54](#cite:54). The inventory remains below its FY2025 level [126](#cite:126), and GAO found the related timeliness statistics systematically understated from 2020 to 2024 [56](#cite:56).

short: Days from initiation to adjudication of a clearance case; DCSA's industry average was 197 days for a Secret and 243 for a Top Secret in FY2026 Q3, against targets of 40 and 75.
definition: End-to-end timeliness is the days from initiation through investigation to adjudication. DCSA's industry cases averaged 197 days for a Secret and 243 for a Top Secret in FY2026 Q3, as averages of all cases under the PMIG-aligned reporting adopted that quarter, not comparable with the 156 and 227 days reported for the fastest 90 percent in FY2026 Q1 [126](#cite:126) [124](#cite:124). The government's targets are 40 days for a moderate-risk and 75 for a high-risk position [54](#cite:54), GAO found the published statistics understated real processing time from 2020 to 2024 [56](#cite:56), and the only phase the firm influences is initiation, 20 to 21 days of the total [126](#cite:126). The controversy record `clearance-timeliness-figures` sets out which figure to plan on [54](#cite:54) [126](#cite:126) [56](#cite:56) [127](#cite:127).

short: The DoD credential for facility and network access: sponsored by a DoD official, issued only after a favorable fingerprint check with an investigation submitted; an interim card does not transfer.
definition: A contractor employee is sponsored for a Common Access Card by a DoD official, and only for both physical access to a DoD facility and network logon, or recurring physical access to multiple facilities for six months or more [138](#cite:138). No card is issued without the required background investigation, at minimum a favorable FBI fingerprint check and a NACI or equivalent submitted to the investigative provider [138](#cite:138); a card may be issued on an interim basis on a favorable National Agency Check, with the final determination on the completed investigation, and interim credentials are not transferable or reciprocally accepted [137](#cite:137). Contractors are registered and re-verified every six months through TASS, and a denial or revocation can be reapplied for after one year [137](#cite:137) [138](#cite:138). An employee credentialed after a completed HSPD-12 investigation is exempt from E-Verify re-verification [128](#cite:128).

short: DoD Manual 8140.03: contracted staff in a cyberspace work role must hold the foundational qualification, by education, training or a listed certification, on the day the work starts.
definition: DoD Manual 8140.03 of February 15, 2023 requires contractors to be fully qualified for the cyberspace work roles they fill, and contracted support personnel to meet the foundational qualification, by education, training or a listed certification, on commencement of the work [139](#cite:139). Government and military personnel have nine months for the foundational and twelve for the resident qualification; anyone unqualified without a waiver is removed from the role, waivers are limited to severe constraints and six months, and twenty hours a year of continuing development are required [139](#cite:139). The manual's implementation ran to three years from February 2023 for all workforce elements [139](#cite:139). The gate `dod-8140-cyber-workforce` binds the clear-start, select and develop stages [139](#cite:139).

short: The principle that access follows a demonstrated need; the pack carries it only as its rules state it: eligibility for access essential to a classified contract, and separate read-ins for SCI and SAP.
definition: The pack's sources do not define need to know by that name. The nearest rule is the one that fixes sponsorship: a contractor may request eligibility only where access is essential to a classified contract, for the minimum number of employees, and never to build a cache of cleared staff [119](#cite:119). Access to particular programs is decided apart from the clearance, with SCI and SAP access on a temporary basis a decision of the granting authority [119](#cite:119), and a temporary Secret is not valid for RD, COMSEC or NATO information until the final grant [119](#cite:119). A non-U.S. citizen receives a Limited Access Authorization only with unique or urgently needed skills and no clearable citizen available [119](#cite:119).

variants: National Industrial Security Program Policy Advisory Committee
short: The National Industrial Security Program Policy Advisory Committee, at whose public meetings DCSA reports industry inventory and timeliness; its slides are the primary behind the clearance clock.
definition: The National Industrial Security Program Policy Advisory Committee holds the public meetings at which DCSA reports industry inventory and timeliness by phase, DHS and DOE report their contractor figures, and the NBIS roadmap is updated; the slides are posted by the Information Security Oversight Office [125](#cite:125). Vendor summaries restate the DCSA figures within days [124](#cite:124) [126](#cite:126), the figures arrive months after the quarter, and the reporting basis changed in FY2026 Q3 [126](#cite:126) [127](#cite:127). The September 2, 2026 slides are the primary behind the 197- and 243-day industry figures, though their chart labels did not survive the fetch and the values are carried from the vendor's report of the same meeting [125](#cite:125) [126](#cite:126).

short: About 4.2 million clearance holders in October 2019, 1.35 million of them contractors or other, on the last public count; the pool is closed because no one can start a clearance alone.
definition: The last public count put about 4.2 million individuals with a security clearance as of October 1, 2019, 2,897,172 government employees and 1,346,765 contractors or other, 672,656 of the latter at top secret [80](#cite:80). The pool is closed in the short run because an individual may not obtain or initiate a security clearance; only a sponsoring agency can [80](#cite:80). The sweep-8 search found no later government count, the 2019 report being the last release of the series, so the indicator `ind-cleared-population-2019` stands with its age stated [80](#cite:80). Within that pool, cleared professionals averaged \$119,131 in total compensation in the 2025 survey, and 13 percent had switched employers for pay in the past year [89](#cite:89).

short: The only route by which a non-U.S. citizen can be cleared, in rare cases and never for Top Secret, RD, COMSEC, intelligence or NATO information.
definition: Under 32 CFR 117.10(k) a non-U.S. citizen can be cleared only by a Limited Access Authorization, in rare cases, only with unique or urgently needed skills and no clearable citizen available, and never for Top Secret, RD, COMSEC, intelligence or NATO information [119](#cite:119). Non-U.S. citizens are ineligible for temporary eligibility [119](#cite:119), and an LAA holder's naturalization is among the events a contractor reports under 32 CFR 117.8 [189](#cite:189). The constraint `c-foreign-national-hire-blocked` sets the authorization beside the export authorization a foreign person needs before working with controlled technical data [132](#cite:132) [131](#cite:131).

short: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics: annual wage and employment estimates by occupation and metro area; May 2025 put software developers at a $148,100 mean.
definition: The Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics program publishes annual wage and employment estimates by occupation, nationally and by metropolitan area; the May 2025 estimates, published May 15, 2026, put software developers at a median of \$65.38 an hour and a mean of \$148,100 a year, and computer and mathematical occupations at 5,260,110 jobs with a mean of \$120,080 [110](#cite:110). It is the series the Service Contract Act wage determinations are generally built from [101](#cite:101). The pay-review and range-setting levers compare a person's pay with the OEWS metro estimate for the SOC code [110](#cite:110), and an OEWS series ID is OE plus the seasonal code, area type, a seven-digit area, six-digit industry, six-digit occupation and a two-digit datatype, whose wage codes the sweep did not read [233](#cite:233).

variants: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey
short: The BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey: monthly openings, hires, quits and layoffs by industry; the pack's demand and churn indicators come from it.
definition: The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey reports monthly openings, hires, quits and layoffs by industry from US nonfarm establishments, seasonally adjusted; the August 2026 release put openings at 7.1 million (4.3 percent), hires at 5.2 million (3.3 percent), quits at 3.1 million (1.9 percent) and layoffs at 1.6 million (1.0 percent), with professional and business services openings at 1,186,000 (5.0 percent), down from 1,305,000 (5.5 percent) in July [57](#cite:57). The pack carries the professional-and-business-services openings rate and the total-nonfarm quits rate as its demand and churn indicators [57](#cite:57). Series IDs are JT plus a seasonal code, a six-digit industry, state, area, size class, a two-character data element and R or L for rate or level, which the BLS format page confirms for JTS540099000000000JOR and JTS000000000000000QUR [230](#cite:230) [235](#cite:235).

short: The BLS quarterly index of wages and benefits: private-industry wages rose 3.1 percent and benefits 3.8 percent in the year to June 2026; the index behind the compensation cap.
definition: The Employment Cost Index is the BLS quarterly index of wages and benefits; in the year to June 2026 private-industry total compensation rose 3.3 percent, wages and salaries 3.1 percent and benefits 3.8 percent, against 3.5, 3.5 and 3.4 percent a year earlier [103](#cite:103). It is the index the OFPP compensation cap uses, the 2025 cap of \$671,000 being the 2024 cap of \$646,000 times the ECI change [107](#cite:107), and the market-escalation evidence a rate-relief request attaches against a labor rate fixed at award [103](#cite:103) [117](#cite:117). The indicator `ind-eci-wages-2026` carries the series CIU2020000000000A, which the BLS guide confirms as private-industry wages and salaries, 12-month percent change, not seasonally adjusted [231](#cite:231).

short: The BLS quarterly measure of cost per hour worked for wages and each benefit; benefits were 30.0 percent of private-industry compensation in June 2026.
definition: Employer Costs for Employee Compensation is the BLS quarterly measure of cost per hour worked for wages and each benefit. In June 2026 private-industry compensation cost \$46.89 an hour, of which wages were \$32.82 (70.0 percent), benefits \$14.07 (30.0 percent) and health insurance \$3.48 (7.4 percent); for management, professional and related occupations the total was \$78.88 with benefits at 31.5 percent [104](#cite:104). The total-rewards lever uses the benefits share to state what a salary leaves out [104](#cite:104). The indicator carries CMU2030000000000P, benefits as a percent of total compensation, with the dollar series CMU2030000000000D over CMU2010000000000D as the fallback [232](#cite:232).

short: The JOLTS openings measure as a rate: 5.0 percent in professional and business services and 4.3 percent economy-wide in August 2026 (preliminary).
definition: The job openings rate is the JOLTS measure the pack carries as its demand indicator: 5.0 percent in professional and business services in August 2026 (preliminary), down from 5.5 percent in July, with the economy-wide openings rate at 4.3 percent, 7.1 million openings against 5.2 million hires [57](#cite:57). The indicator `ind-jolts-pbs-openings-rate` is series JTS540099000000000JOR, whose format the BLS series-ID page confirms [230](#cite:230). The rolling-demand-forecast lever names the public series on openings and shortages among the signals a forecast draws on [57](#cite:57) [71](#cite:71).

short: The JOLTS quits measure as a rate: 1.9 percent of total nonfarm employment, 3.1 million quits, in August 2026 (preliminary); the pack's churn indicator.
definition: The quits rate is the JOLTS churn indicator the pack carries: 1.9 percent of total nonfarm employment in August 2026 (preliminary), 3.1 million quits, in a release that also put openings at 4.3 percent, hires at 3.3 percent and layoffs at 1.0 percent, with quits in professional and business services at 2.1 percent [57](#cite:57). The series is JTS000000000000000QUR, quits rate, total nonfarm, seasonally adjusted, confirmed by the BLS format and the DBnomics listing [230](#cite:230) [235](#cite:235). The retain stage sets it beside the 24.8 percent of newcomers who left one firm within a year as the benchmarks for a voluntary-turnover rate [57](#cite:57) [155](#cite:155).

short: Days to the output the labor category assumes; output rose 53 percent over the first year where it could be counted, and no public benchmark exists for technical staff.
definition: Time to productivity is the onboard-stage metric for the days until a hire reaches the output the labor category assumes. Where output can be counted per worker it rose 53 percent in the first year on the job, with a very steep learning curve, pay profiles much flatter than output for about eighteen months, and the fastest early learners the ones who stayed [157](#cite:157). A labor-category rate assumes qualified, productive hours from the first day [98](#cite:98) and a time-and-materials contract pays only for hours by people who meet the category [99](#cite:99). No public benchmark for the ramp of a technical professional was found; the 53 percent figure is from windshield installers at one company, so the shape transfers and the slope does not [157](#cite:157).

short: A current employer's raised offer to a departing employee; 58 percent of managers extend them and those who accept stay a mean 1.7 years, on a staffing firm's 2018 survey.
definition: A counteroffer is the current employer's bid to keep an employee who has accepted another offer. The only quantitative source found is a staffing firm's 2018 survey of more than 5,500 US managers: 58 percent of senior managers extend counteroffers, and employees who accept one stay a mean 1.7 years [113](#cite:113). No peer-reviewed study of counteroffer outcomes was found, and the figure is carried as survey-grade with its publisher and date [113](#cite:113). The constraint `c-counteroffer-and-withdrawal` sets it among the reasons an accepted offer is not a start, with speed, contact and a package the candidate can compare as the firm's levers [15](#cite:15) [14](#cite:14) [113](#cite:113).

short: A one-time payment on hire; used by 80 percent of organizations and evaluated by 12 percent, and allowable on cost-type work only under a plan that predates the services.
definition: A sign-on bonus is used by 80 percent of organizations and evaluated for effect by 12 percent, on a 2024 practitioner survey, and no study of whether sign-on bonuses work was found in the sweep [118](#cite:118). Under cost-type contracts a bonus is allowable only when paid under an agreement made before the services or a consistently followed plan, and major plan changes need the administrative contracting officer's chance to review [100](#cite:100). California's AB 692 excepts signing bonuses on stated conditions from its bar on repayment terms for contracts entered after January 1, 2026 [167](#cite:167).

short: A payment conditioned on staying; used by 66 percent of organizations, evaluated by 12 percent, and allowable on cost-type work only under an established plan.
definition: Retention bonuses are used by 66 percent of organizations and sign-on bonuses by 80 percent, while 12 percent evaluate whether their bonus programs work, on a 2024 survey; no effectiveness evidence was found [118](#cite:118). On a cost-type contract a retention bonus is allowable only under an agreement or plan established before the services, with major plan changes subject to the administrative contracting officer's review [100](#cite:100).
