A term that makes the worker repay a retention amount on leaving before a date is, for California contracts entered after January 1, 2026, unlawful outside the statute's exceptions [167](#cite:167), and the turnover evidence puts pay itself at ρ −.17 with quitting [178](#cite:178).

short: An offer that states benefits and arrangements in dollars and terms a candidate can compare; benefits are 30 percent of compensation cost and arrangements are priced at 8 to 20 percent of pay.
definition: A total-rewards statement puts the whole package and the arrangement in the offer, in dollars and terms candidates can compare. Benefits are 30.0 percent of private-industry compensation cost and 31.5 percent for management and professional occupations [104](#cite:104); a family health premium averaged \$26,993 in 2025 with the worker paying \$6,850 [105](#cite:105); workers value a work-from-home option at about 8 percent of wages and would give up about 20 percent to avoid employer-set, short-notice schedules [115](#cite:115); working conditions are a central part of compensation in their own right [94](#cite:94). The lever record notes that noncash value does not offset a material base-pay gap [63](#cite:63) and that the 41 percent of small firms offering no health coverage have nothing to state on that line [105](#cite:105).

short: External hires started about 18 percent above workers promoted into similar jobs at one financial-services firm, performed worse for two years and left more often.
definition: The external hire premium is the finding, from personnel records of the US investment-banking arm of a financial-services firm from 2003 to 2009, that external hires into comparable jobs started about 18 percent higher than workers promoted into them, while the promoted workers significantly outperformed the external hires for two years and had lower voluntary and involuntary exit [93](#cite:93). The pack uses it as the premium a larger employer can put on the firm's trained and cleared engineer [93](#cite:93), as the comparison point every market-rate hire sets for incumbents [93](#cite:93) [92](#cite:92), and as the case for the internal route in the equity-review lever [93](#cite:93). It is one firm's record, so the direction, not the magnitude, is what the records carry [93](#cite:93).

short: The pay a worker gives up for an arrangement, or demands to accept one: about 8 percent of wages for a work-from-home option and about 20 percent to avoid short-notice schedules.
definition: A compensating differential is the wage a worker trades for a job's conditions. In a discrete-choice experiment with job seekers in a national call center's hiring process, the average worker would give up about 8 percent of wages for the option to work from home and about 20 percent to avoid an employer-set, short-notice schedule, and while most workers would pay nothing for general scheduling flexibility, a minority with high valuations creates large compensating differentials [115](#cite:115). Working conditions are a central part of compensation, with willingness to pay varying by group and across the wage distribution [94](#cite:94). The retain-stage constraint `c-onsite-schedule-and-commute` carries the two figures as the arrangements an onsite, fixed-schedule job cannot offer [115](#cite:115).

short: What workers say an arrangement is worth in pay: a mean 8 percent for two to three work-from-home days in the SWAA; 8 and 20 percent for home working and predictable schedules in the experiment.
definition: Amenity valuations are the pay-equivalents workers place on arrangements. Respondents to the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes would give up a mean 8 percent of pay for the option to work from home two or three days a week, 29 percent of paid full days were at home in December 2023, and 239 of 470 surveyed firms expanded or plan to expand remote work to keep employees and moderate wage growth [70](#cite:70) [69](#cite:69). The field experiment put the work-from-home option at about 8 percent of wages and avoiding an employer-set, short-notice schedule at about 20 percent [115](#cite:115). The indicator `ind-wfh-valuation` carries the 8 percent figure for the attract, offer and retain stages [70](#cite:70).

short: The web of links, fit and sacrifice that makes leaving costly; corrected correlation −.26 with voluntary turnover across 29 studies, with on-the-job embeddedness the more predictive half.
definition: Job embeddedness is the web of links, fit and sacrifice, on and off the job, that makes leaving costly [192](#cite:192). It predicts voluntary turnover at a corrected ρ of −.26 across 29 studies in the 316-study meta-analysis [178](#cite:178); on-the-job embeddedness is more predictive than off-the-job, and embeddedness is moderately predictive of turnover and minimally of performance [192](#cite:192). At one financial-services firm, on-the-job embeddedness predicted lower turnover within a year (OR 0.42) and partly carried the effect of investiture onboarding tactics [155](#cite:155). The practices suggested to build it, teams, gatherings, fit and flexible scheduling, are untested [192](#cite:192).

short: Thoughts of quitting and intentions to leave; the strongest predictor of voluntary turnover, ρ .56 across 211 studies, with job search next at .40.
definition: Withdrawal cognitions, the wanting-to-leave that precedes leaving, are the strongest predictor of voluntary turnover in the 316-study meta-analysis, at a corrected ρ of .56 across 211 studies, with job search next at .40 across 27 [178](#cite:178). They sit above commitment (−.29), fit (−.29), satisfaction (−.28), embeddedness (−.26), leadership (−.24) and perceived alternatives (.23), and alternatives matter more where withdrawal cognitions are high [178](#cite:178). At the unit level, turnover intentions correlate .34 with turnover rates [181](#cite:181). The retain stage treats voiced intentions and job search as its two leading indicators, heard in check-ins or measured by survey [178](#cite:178).

short: Turnover measured at the unit or firm level; across 82 studies it correlates about −.22 with customer satisfaction and production efficiency and −.15 with profit margin.
definition: Collective turnover is turnover measured as a rate for a unit or a firm. Across 694 effect sizes from 82 studies, turnover rates correlate about −.22 with customer satisfaction and production efficiency, −.15 with profit margin, +.14 with error and loss rates and +.27 with counterproductivity, with other financial measures not significant, and the relationships do not vary between voluntary and total turnover [181](#cite:181). The practices most tied to lower unit turnover are firm-specific training (−.40), internal mobility (−.25), staffing selectivity (−.24) and high-commitment HR systems (−.23), while straight pay, variable pay, staffing levels and general training are not significant [181](#cite:181). The pack carries the figures in `ind-collective-turnover-performance-2013` for the retain, handover and plan stages [181](#cite:181).

short: What replacing a departed employee costs as a share of salary: a 21 percent median across 27 case studies, 16 percent for jobs under $30,000 and up to 213 percent at the top.
definition: The replacement cost is the measured cost of replacing a worker as a share of annual salary: a median of about 21 percent across 27 case studies excluding executives and physicians, 16 percent for jobs paying \$30,000 or less, up to 213 percent for very highly paid roles, a range of 5.8 to 213 percent, with only 2 of 11 papers counting indirect costs [180](#cite:180). Replacement costs are substantial and largest in thin labor markets and for specialized skills, where a worker's unexpected death also raises the remaining same-occupation workers' wages [193](#cite:193). The retain-stage metric `replacement-cost` counts separation, replacement, training and lost productivity per departure [180](#cite:180) [193](#cite:193).

short: The disputed figure for what a departure costs: practitioner multiples of 90 to 200 percent of salary name no study, against a measured case-study median near a fifth.
definition: The cost of turnover is the subject of the controversy record `cost-of-turnover`: trade literature puts direct costs at 50 to 60 percent of salary and total costs at 90 to 200 percent, stated without a named study [195](#cite:195), while the case-study review puts the median replacement cost at 21 percent of annual salary [180](#cite:180). The unit-level evidence measures the cost in customer satisfaction and production efficiency (about −.22) and profit margin (−.15) rather than dollars [181](#cite:181), and the death-shock evidence puts it highest for specialized skills in thin markets [193](#cite:193). The practitioner review of turnover misconceptions holds that retention should be managed from the measured predictors [179](#cite:179).

short: Firms promote on current performance even when other traits predict managerial success; a doubling of a manager's prior sales goes with 7.5 percent lower manager value added.
definition: The Peter Principle, as the sales-worker evidence states it, is that firms promote on current performance even when other traits better predict managerial success, and that promoting workers with lower managerial potential is costly [184](#cite:184). On microdata for sales workers at 214 firms, a worker who sells twice as much as a colleague is about 15 percent more likely to be promoted in that month, a doubling of a manager's pre-promotion sales corresponds to a 7.5 percent decline in manager value added measured through subordinates' sales, and workers with more teamwork experience make better managers without being promoted more often [184](#cite:184) [185](#cite:185). The pattern reflects either inefficient promotion or the incentive value of promotion-for-performance [184](#cite:184); the retain stage carries it as the warning on a small firm's one step up [184](#cite:184) [185](#cite:185).

short: The organized ways a firm brings a newcomer in; institutionalized tactics correlate .24 to .40 with adjustment and the social ones, insiders as guides and investiture, .29 to .47.
definition: Socialization tactics are the structured ways an organization brings newcomers in. Across 183 newcomer samples, institutionalized tactics correlate .24 to .40 with social acceptance, role clarity, task mastery and fit, the social tactics .29 to .47, the strongest, content tactics up to .43 with role clarity and context tactics .10 to .30 [152](#cite:152). At one financial-services firm with no standardized orientation, serial tactics, meaning experienced insiders as role models, and investiture, affirming who the newcomer already is, each roughly halved the odds of leaving within a year (OR 0.44 and 0.52), and collective, investiture and fixed tactics predicted on-the-job embeddedness [155](#cite:155). The plain-language summary notes that no causal evidence yet exists [154](#cite:154).

short: The first ninety days, in which the hire learns the role, the tasks and the people; the onboard stage, whose evidence is the socialization meta-analyses and one firm's turnover study.
definition: Onboarding is the onboard stage's work: the first ninety days in which the hire becomes someone who knows the role, can do the tasks and is accepted by the people [152](#cite:152). Structured tactics and the newcomer's own proactivity both predict that adjustment, social acceptance then carries performance (.35), intentions to leave (−.27) and leaving (−.12), and the links from adjustment to actual turnover are small [152](#cite:152). Support from the supervisor and the team fell week by week across fourteen weekly surveys, early support predicted integration and commitment at ninety days, and an undermining supervisor tripled the hazard of leaving (HR 3.01) [156](#cite:156); at one firm with no standardized orientation 24.8 percent of newcomers left within a year [155](#cite:155). The lever `l-structured-onboarding-program` writes the first week, month and quarter down with an insider beside the hire [152](#cite:152) [155](#cite:155) [156](#cite:156).

short: Role clarity, task mastery and social acceptance, the three things a newcomer has to acquire; they mediate the path from tactics to satisfaction, commitment, performance and staying.
definition: Newcomer adjustment is the three-part state the socialization model turns on: role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance, which mediated the effects of tactics and information seeking on satisfaction, commitment, performance, intentions to remain and turnover across 70 samples in the 2007 meta-analysis [153](#cite:153). In the 2025 update of 183 samples, with task mastery in place of self-efficacy, social acceptance relates to satisfaction at .42, commitment .40, performance .35, turnover intentions −.27 and turnover −.12; role clarity to satisfaction .38 and performance .23; task mastery to performance .38; and perceived fit to satisfaction .46 and turnover intentions −.31 [152](#cite:152). The onboard-stage metric `ninety-day-integration` measures the three at ninety days, where early support predicts them [152](#cite:152) [153](#cite:153) [156](#cite:156).

short: An experienced insider beside the newcomer; the strongest onboarding tactic for the firm, with small measurable career gains for the protégé and a cost in senior billable hours.
definition: Mentoring, an experienced insider beside the newcomer, is among the social tactics that correlate .29 to .47 with adjustment, the strongest of any, and it relates to role clarity more strongly in horizontal-individualistic cultures (.38 against .17) [152](#cite:152). For the protégé the measurable gains are modest: mentoring is associated with objective outcomes such as compensation and promotions with small effect sizes and with larger subjective ones [164](#cite:164), and across youth, academic and workplace settings the effect is generally small [165](#cite:165). The cost is the senior's time, which on a time-and-materials contract is a contract hour forgone or an indirect hour added to the rates [99](#cite:99) [148](#cite:148); learning from more knowledgeable coworkers is itself worth 4 to 9 percent of total compensation [158](#cite:158).

short: Whether a trained skill is used on the job; supported by realistic practice, a supervisor who expects it (ρ .31), a transfer climate (.37) and an early chance to perform.
definition: Transfer of training is whether a trained skill is used on the job. The review finds the most consistent support for cognitive ability (ρ .43), self-efficacy, motivation to transfer (.43 against .07 for motivation to learn), perceived utility, behavioral modelling, error management and realistic training environments, a transfer climate (.37), supervisor support (.31 against .14 for peer support), opportunity to perform and follow-up [162](#cite:162). The often-repeated estimate that only 10 percent of training spending transfers is a 1982 figure the review repeats, not a measurement [162](#cite:162). Motivation and self-efficacy matter more for open skills, the ones performed differently each time, than for closed skills [163](#cite:163). The meta-analytic coefficients are carried from the review; the meta-analyses themselves are todos [162](#cite:162).

short: Skills any employer can use; theory says the worker should pay for them, the evidence says firms do, because the training firm knows the worker's ability better than the market.
definition: General human capital is skill a worker can take to any employer. Standard theory says workers pay for general training because it raises their value everywhere; the observed fact is that firms pay for it, which the economics explains by the training firm's superior information about the worker's ability, an ex post monopsony that makes paying for general skills worthwhile, with the economy able to sit in a low-training, high-quit equilibrium or a high-training, low-quit one [161](#cite:161). A one-point rise in training raises value added per hour about 0.6 percent and hourly wages about 0.3 percent on British industry data, so the firm keeps part of the return while the worker stays [159](#cite:159). Tuition reimbursement raised retention at one establishment, but 80 percent of the effect came through who sorted into the firm [160](#cite:160); at the unit level general training is not significantly related to turnover rates [181](#cite:181).

short: Skill of use mainly to the current firm; firm-specific training is the practice most strongly tied to lower unit turnover, ρ −.40 across the unit-level studies.
definition: Specific human capital is skill of use mainly to the firm that supplied it. Firm-specific training is the practice most strongly associated with lower unit turnover (−.40) across 82 studies, ahead of internal mobility (−.25) and staffing selectivity (−.24), while general training is not significant [181](#cite:181). The economics of why a firm trains at all rests on the training firm's information advantage rather than on specificity: the employer who trained someone knows what they can do better than the market does and keeps part of the return [161](#cite:161). The embeddedness-building lever names investment in firm-specific skills and tools as the training that keeps units together [181](#cite:181).

short: A prime, customer or competitor hiring the person the firm trained and cleared; agreements not to do so are criminal, so the hold has to be in the job.
definition: Poaching is the hiring of the firm's trained and cleared person by the prime, the customer or a competitor. External hires are paid about 18 percent more than internal promotees for comparable jobs, the premium a larger employer can put on the firm's engineer [93](#cite:93), and 13 percent of cleared professionals switched employers for pay in a year [89](#cite:89). The firm cannot answer it with an agreement: agreements between competing employers not to recruit, solicit or hire each other's workers are illegal even without actual harm and may be prosecuted as felonies, and a non-solicitation term survives only as a subordinate, collateral and reasonably necessary part of a legitimate collaboration [187](#cite:187); the federal noncompete rule is vacated and the state rules vary [169](#cite:169). What holds people is what the turnover evidence says holds them: embeddedness (ρ −.26), commitment, fit and the supervisor [178](#cite:178), and firm-specific training at the unit level (−.40) [181](#cite:181).

short: Hiring from employees' networks; referred workers quit 10 to 30 percent less across nine firms, and the networks are segregated, so the pool narrows as it improves.
definition: Referral hiring draws candidates from employees' networks. Across nine large firms in three industries, referred applicants were substantially more likely to be hired and referred workers 10 to 30 percent less likely to quit, about 13 percent in call centers, 12 percent in trucking and 30 percent in high-tech, with little difference on most productivity measures, gains in rare events such as accidents and patents, and referrals from above-median workers worth far more (\$4,190 of discounted profit in trucking) than those from below-median workers (\$1,063) [60](#cite:60). At one financial-services firm referred applicants were 7.3 points more likely to be interviewed and 2.4 points more likely to be offered, and referred workers about 15 percent less likely to leave [61](#cite:61). Referral networks are segregated, so firms hire and retain people who resemble the founders' networks until cumulative hires dilute the effect [81](#cite:81); a referral also lowered the odds that an accepted hire never started (OR 0.42) [144](#cite:144).

short: What candidates believe the firm is as an employer; favorable images relate to better recruitment outcomes and form through recruiters and word of mouth.
definition: Employer image is the set of beliefs candidates hold about the firm as an employer, defined apart from reputation and identity and measured as attributes or as overall attractiveness; favorable images relate to better recruitment outcomes, stronger emotional bonds, differentiation and financial returns, and they form from organizational sources, the recruiters, and non-organizational ones, word of mouth [64](#cite:64). Job and organization characteristics, recruiter behaviors, process perceptions, perceived fit and hiring expectancies predict attraction and job choice across 667 coefficients from 71 studies, while recruiter demographics do not [63](#cite:63). Half of organizations report losing talent to competitors [43](#cite:43).

short: Masculine-coded words in job ads, near-universal for male-dominated jobs, lower women's rated appeal and belonging for the same job without changing perceived skill requirements.
definition: Gendered wording is the use of masculine- or feminine-coded words in job advertisements. In two archival studies, 493 online ads in 11 occupations and 3,640 university co-op ads, ads for male-dominated jobs carried more masculine-coded words, 97 percent against 70 percent of professional ads for female-dominated jobs; in three experiments women rated masculine-worded versions of the same ad less appealing (4.16 against 4.50 of 6) and felt less belonging (3.98 against 4.31 of 7), men were unaffected, and perceived skill requirements were unchanged [77](#cite:77). The posting-rewrite lever strips such words along with the age terms the ADEA regulations list, young and recent college graduate among them [77](#cite:77) [78](#cite:78).

short: Replacing credential lines with skill requirements; announced at scale, it changed who was hired by less than one in 700 because the screens did not change.
definition: Skills-based hiring replaces degree and years-of-experience requirements with named skills. Roles dropping degree requirements rose almost fourfold from 2014 to 2023, yet non-degree hiring in those roles rose only 3.5 percentage points and the economy-wide effect was less than one hire in 700, with firms sorting into Leaders, In Name Only and Backsliders; the non-degree hires made stayed longer [68](#cite:68) [58](#cite:58). Nearly 70 percent of campus-recruiting employers say they use it [79](#cite:79), and 88 percent of surveyed employers report their systems reject qualified high-skilled candidates for not matching criteria exactly [44](#cite:44). The controversy record `skills-based-hiring` concludes that the announcement is not the practice and that the posting changes hiring only when the screen and the assessment change with it [68](#cite:68) [44](#cite:44) [1](#cite:1).

short: A credential line in a posting; it shrinks the pool for little validity, since years of experience predicts performance at .07 and education was excluded for lack of data.
definition: A degree requirement is a credential line in the posting. Years of job experience predicts performance at .07 and years of education was excluded for insufficient data in the 2022 re-estimation of selection validity [1](#cite:1). Roles dropping degree requirements rose almost fourfold from 2014 to 2023 while non-degree hiring in them rose only 3.5 percentage points, and the non-degree hires made stayed longer [68](#cite:68). The plan-stage constraint `c-preferences-written-as-requirements` notes that a degree or years figure the labor category does not require cannot be traced to the contract [99](#cite:99) [68](#cite:68), and a requirement with adverse impact must be job-related and consistent with business necessity [30](#cite:30) [32](#cite:32).

short: A person not actively searching for a job; the author's ledger row says strong candidates are not searching, and the evidence says such people are reached through networks and referrals.
definition: A passive candidate is a person who is not actively searching for a job. The ledger row `h-A3` carries the author's hypothesis that strong candidates are not actively searching and are reached through technical networks, referrals and targeted outreach; the sweep found it supported in that people not actively searching are reached through networks, since referred applicants are more likely to be interviewed and hired and referred workers quit 10 to 30 percent less [60](#cite:60) [61](#cite:61). The pathfinder's role condition `rare-skill-or-passive-market` tags the constraints that bind when the skill is rare or the market is mostly passive candidates. The trade-off the row names, sustained effort with results that may arrive too late for an immediate vacancy, is marked as a synthesis with no study behind it.

short: Acquisition spend per hire as SHRM defines it; medians of $1,200 for nonexecutive and $10,625 for executive hires in 2025, with agency fees among the components.
definition: Cost per hire is the acquisition spend per hire: SHRM defines it as the costs of a new hire, agency fees, job boards, referral costs, travel, relocation, recruiter pay and benefits and systems, divided by hires, and reports 2025 medians of \$1,200 for nonexecutive roles, down 27 percent since 2017, and \$10,625 for executive roles, up 113 percent, from a survey of 2,371 members [196](#cite:196). ISO/TS 30407 is the technical specification that defines the metric, beside impact of hire (30410), quality of hire (30411) and succession metrics (33433) [46](#cite:46). The plan stage treats it as the one of three requisition costs that shows on an invoice, beside the vacancy's cost and the cash fronted before payment [196](#cite:196) [180](#cite:180) [202](#cite:202).

short: The record of one opening to be filled; small organizations run a median of six per recruiter, and the plan stage asks whether each is funded, defined and priced before it is posted.
definition: A requisition is the firm's record of one opening. Small organizations under 100 employees run a median of six requisitions per recruiter and filled every executive and nonexecutive position externally in 2025 [196](#cite:196). The plan stage asks of each whether it is real, a clearance being requestable only for a contract need [119](#cite:119) and a proposed key person reportable if unavailable [108](#cite:108); what it is, with the labor category's line the enforceable definition of qualified [99](#cite:99); and what it costs, in acquisition spend, vacancy cost and cash fronted before a 30-day payment [196](#cite:196) [180](#cite:180) [202](#cite:202). The scorecard lever labels each requirement as contractual, customer-required in writing, or preferred [99](#cite:99) [197](#cite:197).

short: One accountable person who owns a requisition from opening to first productive day, with the calendar of every clock on it; the practice is unstudied.
definition:
<!-- synthesis -->
A requisition owner is the one person the lever `l-one-requisition-owner` names to own an opening from posting to first productive day, with the authority to decide and the calendar of every clock on it: the posting, the screen, the interview, the offer, the customer's review, the sponsorship, the credential and the start. The evidence is on the delays the owner is meant to prevent: earlier offers are accepted more often with no later penalty [15](#cite:15), candidates who withdraw differ in how they perceived the process [16](#cite:16), and each week between acceptance and start raised the odds of a no-show by 22 percent [144](#cite:144). Whether a single owner shortens the clocks has not been studied; the ledger closes row E1 as unstudied, and small organizations run a median of six requisitions per recruiter [196](#cite:196).

short: Long-term strategies for acquiring, developing and retaining the workforce, in GAO's definition; the five principles are the reference shape for a firm's rolling forecast.
definition: Strategic workforce planning, in GAO's 2003 definition, is developing long-term strategies for acquiring, developing and retaining the total workforce, under five principles: involve top management, employees and other stakeholders; determine the critical skills and competencies needed for current and future results; develop strategies tailored to gaps in number, deployment and alignment; build the capability to support them; and monitor and evaluate progress [205](#cite:205). The principles are guidance written for federal agencies, not evidence of effect, and the pack carries them as the reference shape for a rolling forecast at a firm that has none [205](#cite:205). The clocks a plan buys time against are the 45-day median fill [43](#cite:43) and the 197-to-243-day clearance [126](#cite:126).

short: A dated list of expected openings by labor category, contract and probability, kept so the pipelines exist before the vacancies open; no study of forecast accuracy at small contractors was found.
definition: A demand forecast is the lever `l-rolling-demand-forecast`: a dated list of expected openings by labor category, contract and probability, revised quarterly, with the pipelines for recurring skills maintained before the vacancies open. The planning principles ask for the critical skills, the gaps, the capability and the measure [205](#cite:205); the signals are the firm's own pipeline and the public series on openings and shortages, 5.0 percent openings in professional and business services and 87 percent of small firms hiring reporting few or no qualified applicants [57](#cite:57) [71](#cite:71). The constraint `c-no-forecast-until-urgent` records that a firm starting at the vacancy faces a 45-day median fill [43](#cite:43) or a 197-to-243-day clearance clock [126](#cite:126) from a standing start, that no study of forecast accuracy in small contractors was found, and that a cache of cleared people cannot be built in any case [119](#cite:119).

short: What an open requisition costs: unbilled hours, delivery at risk, strain on the people covering it and the replacement cost, about a fifth of salary in the case-study median.
definition:
<!-- synthesis -->
The vacancy cost is the plan-stage estimate of what an open requisition costs, in the four parts the lever `l-vacancy-cost-estimate` names: unbilled hours, the contract's missing revenue on a time-and-materials contract [99](#cite:99); delivery at risk, with unit turnover at about −.22 with customer satisfaction and production efficiency [181](#cite:181); the strain on the people covering it, which predicts quitting through stress (ρ .21), role conflict (.15) and work–life conflict (.19) where hours as such do not (−.10) [178](#cite:178); and the replacement cost, about 21 percent of salary in the case-study median and far more for the highly paid [180](#cite:180). The estimate needs assumptions, unbilled revenue is not lost profit, and no study of vacancy prioritization was found.

short: Carrying payroll before the funded work it was hired for begins; the payroll is indirect cost in the firm's rates, and a clearance cannot be requested ahead of a contract need.
definition:
<!-- synthesis -->
Hiring ahead is making a hire before the first invoice on the work the person was hired for. The payroll before billing is indirect cost, pooled and allocated through the firm's rates [148](#cite:148); a proper invoice is paid 30 days after receipt by default [202](#cite:202), with a 15-day goal for small business contractors [201](#cite:201); and a clearance cannot be requested ahead of a contract need in any case [119](#cite:119). The lever `l-hiring-ahead-exposure-cap` sets a limit on the people and months of payroll carried before the first invoice and stages developmental and sponsored hires against it, at the cost of a slower response when work arrives [148](#cite:148) [202](#cite:202). The bridge-work lever asks what a sponsored hire will do, and who pays, while the clearance runs [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99) [148](#cite:148).

short: Funded work identified for a sponsored hire while the clearance runs; contract hours are paid only for qualified labor on the contract, so other payroll is the firm's indirect cost.
definition:
<!-- synthesis -->
Bridge work is the funded work the lever `l-bridge-work-plan` asks a firm to identify before a sponsored hire is made, for the wait between the start and the clearance. Contract hours are paid only for qualified labor performed on the contract [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99); other payroll is an indirect cost allocated through the firm's pools and rates [148](#cite:148); whether unclassified contract work is open to an uncleared hire depends on the contract's security terms [146](#cite:146); and the hire cannot be sponsored ahead of a contract need to shorten the wait [119](#cite:119). The wait runs 197 to 243 days on the current industry figures [126](#cite:126). No study of bridge-work practice or of its effect on whether hires stay through the wait was found; the only evidence on the wait itself is that financial security lowered the odds of a no-show (OR 0.86) and a competing offer raised them (OR 1.18) [144](#cite:144).

short: Days from acceptance to the first productive day; each additional week raised the odds of a no-show by 22 percent among 157,154 accepted offers at one employer.
definition: The offer-to-start interval is the clear-start stage's metric: days from acceptance to the first productive day. Among 157,154 accepted entry-level offers at one telecommunications employer from May 2019 to June 2025, 4.1 percent of hires never showed up, and each additional week between acceptance and the start date raised the odds of a no-show (OR 1.22), while a referral (OR 0.42), good company communication (OR 0.56) and financial security (OR 0.86) lowered them and an external offer raised them (OR 1.18) [144](#cite:144). A cleared opening stretches the interval to the clearance clock, 197 to 243 days on the current industry figures [126](#cite:126), and a key-personnel hire to an award date the firm does not set [108](#cite:108). The population is entry-level and customer-facing, so the rates do not transfer to cleared technical hiring; the mechanism does [144](#cite:144).
